FACT: ■

The petitioner-assessee had advanced a loan to Ninex at an agreed rate of interest and interest was remitted to assessee, albeit, after deducting tax at source by Ninex. When the assessee filed its return of income, it initially did not claim credit for the tax at source deducted and credit for tax at source was claimed by the assessee in its revised return.

■

The revised return was processed under section 143(1), whereby the credit for tax at source was disallowed.

■

An application under section 154 was filed and the same was rejected.In order to get credit of tax at source deducted by Ninex, the assessee had preferred a representation which was, however, rejected with the observation that as per Form 26AS no credit was reflecting.

■

In instant writ petition, the assessee had sought a direction for being given credit of tax deducted at source by Ninex.

HELD: ■

Ninex is, presently, undergoing a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (“CIRP”). It is also not in dispute that the Resolution Professional (“RP”) has issued a certificate dated 05-01-2021 evidencing that Tax at Source (TAS) amounting to Rs.26,99,950/-, was, in fact, deducted against interest paid by Ninex qua the loan extended to it. [Paras 13 and 14]

■

No recovery towards Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) can be made against the petitioner i.e., the deductee, in view of the provisions of section 205. [Para 21]

■

Insofar as the second issue is concerned, the argument advanced on behalf of the revenue is that no credit for tax can be given having regard to the provisions of section 199. In other words, the submission is that unless the tax deducted at source is “paid” to the Central Government, no credit can be given to the deductee, i.e., the petitioner in this case. As would be evident upon perusing the judgment rendered in Sanjay Sudan v. Asstt. CIT [2023] 148 taxmann.com 329/292 Taxman 138/452 ITR 107 (Delhi) this very submission was rejected. [Para 21.1]

■

Since repeated arguments are raised by the revenue based on the provisions of section 199, the rationale provided in Sanjay Sudan’s case is required to be elaborated. It is required to be emphasized that deduction of taxes at source is one of the methods of collecting tax. The TDS deducted at source is part of the assessee’s income and, therefore, the gross amount is included in the total income and offered to tax. It is on this premise that the tax deducted at source would have to be treated as tax paid on behalf of the assessee. The TDS is deducted prior to the assessment being completed. Thus, it is only when the relevant previous year is over, can the assessee’s total income from all sources be determined. Upon assessment of the total income, amongst others, credit for tax deducted at source is extended to an assessee. If the tax assessed is more than the tax deducted at source, the assessee is granted refund. However, if the tax assessed is less than the tax dedudcted at source, the assessee, i.e., the deductee is liable to pay the deficit amount. [Para 21.2]

FACT: The assessee won two lottery prizes during the period relevant to the assessment year 1986-87. The agency, while making payment of prize money to the assessee, deducted the tax at source but did not deposit the money so deducted in the Government treasury. According to the agency, in absence of relevant records having been forwarded to the Chairman, Vaibhavshali Bumper, they were not able to furnish the date of payment of taxes to the treasury. The Assessing Officer rejected the agency's explanation and, while making assessment, did not give credit for the TDS to the assessee but observed that the credit for this would be given only when evidence as to actual payment of the same was produced.

The Assessing Officer issued two notices under section 226(3) to the assessee's bankers directing them to pay the dues forthwith, failing which usual consequences under different sections of the Act would follow.

On writ, the assessee impugned the orders/notices of attachment and prayed for a direction to the Assessing Officer to give credit for TDS The Single Judge set aside the impugned order holding it to be contrary to the provisions of section 205.

On appeal :

HELD: On facts, it appeared to be a case where, in all probability, the amount was deducted at source by the agency from the prize money payable to the assessee but the same did not seem to have been made over to the Government treasury for payment to the Central Government.

A certificate of deduction is to be provided by the person deducting the tax as provided under section 203. There is a bar against direct demand on the assessee where the tax is deducted at source as provided under section 205. The assessee is not supposed to do any thing in the whole transaction except that he has to accept the payment of the reduced amount from which is deducted income-tax at source. The responsibility to deposit the amount deducted at source as tax is that of the person who is responsible to deduct the tax at source. On the amount being deducted, the assessee only gets a certificate to that effect by the person responsible to deduct the tax. In a case where the amount has been deducted by the person responsible to deduct the amount under the statutory provisions, the assessee has no control over the matter. In case of default in making over the amount to the account of the Central Government, it is obviously the person responsible to deduct or the person who has made the deduction who is held responsible for the same. The responsibility of such person is to the extent that he has to be deemed to be an assessee-in-default in respect of the tax.

FACT: The assessee derived salary income from a company for which he worked from October 2000 to January 2002 and also received professional fees from another company. Since assessee’s employers deducted tax at source (TDS), from such payment made by them, he claimed credit thereof in his return accordingly. The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the same on the ground that the assessee did not possess the requisite TDS certificate. On appeal, since the assessee could not produce the evidence of TDS deduction except the bank statements and some payslips, the Commissioner (Appeals) could not grant relief to the assessee. He, however, directed the Assessing Officer to verify from the TDS wing to establish whether the payers actually deducted the tax and/or filed the TDS return or not. He was also directed to give full credit of the TDS made on the basis of such verification report in case the same was found positive. The Commissioner (Appeals) alternatively directed the Assessing Officer that in case, the credit for TDS could not be made, at least the corresponding receipts should be reduced so that only the net receipts credited in the bank account be treated as the gross receipts on which the assessee might agree to pay the taxes again.

On cross appeal :

HELD: The assessee had filed few payslips that was for the month of April to July 2001 and from its perusal, it appeared that TDS was deducted at the time of payment and the net amount showed in the payslips was credited to the bank account of the assessee. From Form No. 16 filed by the assessee it was found that the TDS deducted was paid in April to July 2001. But the figures of deposit did not correlate with the TDS deducted as per the payslips. From the perusal of the bank statement and payslip, it appeared that net payment was credited to the bank statements month after month i.e., up to August 2001. But from the perusal of payslip and the bank statement, an inference could only be drawn that TDS might have been deducted on payment of salary and the professional fees to the assessee. But, it could not be called to be a conclusive proof, for grant of credit of the same. No doubt it is a settled position of law that once the TDS is deducted, it becomes the liability of the deductor and the assessee or the deductee cannot be fastened with the same liability. The Commissioner (Appeals) had directed the Assessing Officer, to verify from the TDS Wing to establish whether the payers actually deducted the tax and filed the TDS return or not. If yes, the Assessing Officer was directed to give full credit of the TDS made on the basis of such verification report from the said Wing of the Department. There was no error in the direction of the Commissioner (Appeals) under the given facts and circumstances of the case. If it was established that TDS was deducted, the full credit be given to the assessee and recovery be made from the employers in that regard according to the law as they were the defaulters and not the assessee. There was also force in the direction given by the Commissioner (Appeals) to the Assessing Officer to treat the net receipts credited in the bank as gross receipts and compute the tax liability thereon. Therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals), was to be confirmed. Accordingly, the appeal of the assessee as well as the revenue would stand dismissed. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 205, read with sections 192, 199 and 203, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection and recovery of tax - Bar against direct demand on assessee - Assessment year 1996-97 - Whether in view of section 205, income-tax authorities, under no circumstances, can make assessee liable to make payment of any tax to extent to which tax has been deducted at source by person paying salary to assessee under section 192 - Held, yes - Whether, however, at same time, credit for tax deducted at source cannot be given to assessee unless he submits certificate as prescribed under section 203 in 
 respect of TDS as per provisions of section 199 - Held, yes - Whether till powers available to income-tax authorities to enforce payment of tax by deductor and also enforce issue of certificate in respect thereof to payee were not exercised by revenue authorities to corner deductor of tax, no tax as well as interest pertaining thereto could be recovered from assessee - Held, yes.

FACT: The assessee’s employer paid salary to him after deducting the tax therefrom. But despite repeated requests made by the assessee, his employer did not furnish the requisite TDS certificate. Consequently, he filed his return without Form No. 16 and also requested the Assessing Officer to enforce the issue of said certificate by the employer in exercise of his jurisdiction over the matter. However, in the absence of the same, the Assessing Officer framed the assessment under section 143(1)(a) raising tax demand in respect of salary income which was levied for the TDS certificate not furnished as well as interest payable in respect of the said tax. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that in the absence of Form No. 16 and Form No. 24, giving credit for TDS on salary did not appear to be justified, though the assessee could not be asked to pay the tax again to the extent to which tax had already been deducted in view of section 205. He, accordingly, directed the Assessing Officer to ask the assessee to obtain the same from the employer and furnish the same.

On second appeal :

HELD: Tax had been deducted from the salary of the assessee by the employer. In this view of the factual position, section 205 really put a bar against direct demand on the assessee. The interest leviable in respect of TDS also is a consequence of non-furnishing of certificate by the assessee in respect of TDS. Had the employer given the assessee a TDS certificate, no interest could be levied on the assessee as the same was to be reduced while computing assessed tax. However, at the same time, credit for tax deducted at source cannot be given to an assessee unless the assessee submits certificate as prescribed under section 203 in respect of TDS as per provisions of section 199. [Para 5]

Hence, in view of section 205, the authorities under no circumstances could make the assessee liable to make payment of any tax to the extent to which the tax had been deducted at source by the person paying the salary to the assessee under section 192. However, as TDS certificate had not been given by deductor, the credit of TDS could not be given. Under the peculiar circumstances of the case, the income-tax authorities were directed not to recover any tax levied on the assessee in respect of non-furnishing of TDS certificate. There are various provisions in the Act which provide the powers to the income-tax authorities to enforce the payment of tax by deductor and also enforce issue of certificate in respect thereof to the payee. There was no material on record to show that whether such powers had been exercised by the department to enforce the payment of tax deducted at source and also for the issue of certificate thereof. In that view of the situation, the assessee could not be held liable for the consequences which were beyond the control of the assessee, i.e., non-furnishing of TDS certificate. Till such powers were not exercised by the revenue authorities to corner the deductor of tax, i.e., to collect payment of TDS from him and also to obtain the certificate, no tax as well as interest pertaining thereto could be recovered from the assessee. The appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed in the aforesaid terms. [Para 6]

Though Form 26AS (read with rule 31AB and sections 203AA and 206C(5)) represents a part of a wholesome procedure designed by the Revenue for accounting of TDS (and TCS), the burden of proving as to why the said Form (Statement) does not reflect the details of the entire tax deducted at source for and on behalf of a deductee cannot be placed on an assessee-deductee. The assessee, by furnishing the TDS certificate/s bearing the full details of the tax deducted at source, credit for which is being claimed, has discharged the primary onus on it toward claiming credit in its respect. He, accordingly, cannot be burdened any further in the matter. The revenue is fully entitled to conduct proper verification in the matter and satisfy itself with regard to the veracity of the assessee’s claim/s, but cannot deny the assessee credit in respect of TDS without specifying any infirmity in its claim/s.

Form 26AS is a statement generated at the end of the revenue, and the assessee cannot be in any manner held responsible for any discrepancy therein or for the non-matching of TDS reflected therein with the assessee’s claim/s. Where so, no doubt a matter of concern, is one which is to be investigated and pursued by the revenue, which is suitably armed by law therefor. The plea that the deductor may have specified a wrong TAN, so that the TDS may stand reflected in the account of another deductee, is no reason or ground for not allowing credit for the TDS in the hands of the proper deductee. The onus for the purpose lies squarely at the door of the revenue. [Para 4.3]

Therefore, the revenue is obliged to grant the assessee credit for the TDS of which he is able to satisfactorily prove to the Assessing Officer, the factum of deduction of tax at source and its deposit to the credit of the Central Government, subject of course to the conditions of sections 198 and 199. The Assessing Officer is accordingly directed to allow the assessee credit for the impugned shortfall, subject to the said verification/s and condition/s.

time for taking an action under a particular section largely depends on a host of factors, inter alia, the nature of proceedings; the character of the order, etc. In order to determine the reasonable time for taking an action under section 201, it is important to have a look at such necessary factors. [Para 14.4]

VI. Nature of proceedings under section 201(1)

The following steps are involved in the proceedings for deduction, payment and recovery of tax at source : When a person pays a sum to anyone on which tax is required to be deducted, then the person responsible for paying such sum is under an obligation to deduct tax at source at the time of credit of such sum to the account of the payee or at the time of payment thereof in cash or by issuing of a cheque or by any other mode, whichever is earlier. When the person responsible has deducted the tax and paid it to the credit of the Central Government or as the Board directs him, his duty is over insofar as the question of deduction of tax at source is concerned, of course, subject to the issuance of certificate of such deduction to the payee and the furnishing of the TDS return in time. If, however, such person who is responsible for deducting tax at source fails to deduct the whole or any part of the tax deductible or after deducting fails to pay the same to the exchequer, prima facie, he becomes the assessee-in-default. The very act of not deducting tax at source or failure to deposit the same makes such person as an assessee-in-default. [Paras 15.1 and 15.2]

When there is such a failure as is referred to in the preceding para, the proceedings are launched against the person responsible and inquiry is conducted. If at the conclusion of such proceedings, it is found that the person responsible for paying has failed to deduct tax or has failed to deposit the same after deduction, he or it is deemed to be an assessee-in-default in respect of such tax by way of an order under section 201(1) subject to the prescription of the Explanation to section 191. Thus, this order crystallizes the liability on the person responsible for paying tax which was deductible. Albeit the person responsible for deducting tax at source becomes a defaulter the moment he makes the payment or credits it to the account of the payee, whichever is earlier, without deduction of tax at source, but on the passing of the order under section 201(1), the amount of tax is determined in respect of which such person responsible is deemed to be an assessee-in-default. [Para 15.3]

On the passing of the order under section 201(1), a notice of demand is issued under section 156 in the name of such person who is deemed to be an assessee-in-default, specifying the sum so payable. If the notice of demand is complied with and the sum determined by way of an order under section 201(1), is paid, the matter ends. [Para 15.4]

If, however, there is a failure to comply with the terms of notice of demand issued under section 156, the tax recovery proceedings are initiated. Section 231, prior to its omission by the Direct Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 1987 with effect from 1-4-1989, provided that no proceedings for the recovery of any sum payable under this Act would be commenced after the expiration of three years from the last day of the financial year in which the demand was made or in the case of a person who was deemed to be an assessee-in-default under any provisions of this Act. This section, thus, provides that no proceedings for recovery of any sum payable under this Act shall be commenced after the expiry of three years from the last day of the financial year in which the demand was made. This means that the recovery certificate could be issued by the Assessing Officer only within the aforesaid period of three years. Simultaneous with the omission of section 231, an amendment has been carried out to section 222 by which the requirement of the issue of such certificate by an Assessing Officer has been dispensed with and the TRO can now draw the statement of arrears and assume jurisdiction as soon as the assessee is in default. [Para 15.5]

HEADNOTE: I. Section  199,  read with section  205,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Credit for tax deducted  (Scope of) - Assessment year  2022-23  - Assessee, a law firm, received payments from its clients net of TDS, i.e., deductors withheld applicable TDS before releasing amounts - Assessee claimed credit of TDS while offering entire gross receipts to tax - However, Assessing Officer denied claim solely on ground that such amounts did not feature in Form No. 26AS - Consequently, a demand was raised comprising disallowed TDS together with interest under sections 234B and 234C - It was noted that assessee had demonstrated deduction of tax at source through its invoices and bank statements - Reconciliation placed on record showed deduction by a company which was not deposited owing to company's financial condition - Whether section 205 erects a clear bar against making a direct demand on assessee to extent tax had been deducted at source from his income and moment deduction was shown on strength of primary evidence, embargo of section 205 attaches and deductee could not again be called upon to bear burden - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had already brought corresponding income to tax, denial of credit in assessee's hands, because deductor failed to deposit or misreported deduction, would result in taxing same income twice - Held, yes - Whether thus, assessee was entitled to credit of TDS to extent deduction from its receipts was established on basis of contemporaneous material placed on record - Held, yes [Paras 19, 24 and 27] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section  234B,  read with sections  143,  199  and  234C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Advance tax  -  Interest for default in payment of  (TDS credit) - Assessment year  2022-23  - Assessee, a law firm, filed its return and offered gross receipts to tax, and claimed credit of TDS - However, Assessing Officer denied claim solely on ground that such amounts did not feature in Form No. 26AS - Consequently, a demand was raised comprising disallowed TDS together with interest under sections 234B and 234C - Whether levy of interest under sections 234B and 234C would not survive once credit was allowed - Held, yes - Whether further, when tax liability stands met through TDS and difference was occasioned solely by deductor's lapse, fastening compensatory interest upon deductee would be unjust and contrary to scheme of Act - Held, yes - Whether thus, Assessing Officer was to be directed to delete interest charged under sections 234B and 234C - Held, yes [Para 28] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, law firm, was engaged in providing legal services. The assessee received payments from clients which were net of tax deducted at source, the deductors having withheld the applicable TDS before releasing amounts. The assessee while filing return claimed credit for such deductions while offering the entire gross receipts to tax.

■

The Assessing Officer denied credit of TDS solely on the ground that such amounts did not feature in Form No. 26AS. Consequently, a demand was raised comprising the disallowed TDS together with interest under section 234B and under section 234C.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the denial of credit, holding that unless the deduction appeared in Form 26AS, the assessee could not be allowed relief. As regards levy of interest under sections 234B and 234C, the Commissioner (Appeals) held the same to be consequential and mandatory.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The case turns on a simple but significant proposition. When tax has in fact been deducted at source from the assessee’s receipts, can credit be denied merely because the deductor has not deposited the tax or has not correctly reported it and, therefore, the credit does not surface in Form 26AS. The answer must be in the negative. Section 205 erects a clear bar against making a direct demand on the assessee to the extent tax has been deducted at source from his income. The moment deduction is shown on the strength of primary evidence, the embargo of section 205 attaches and the deductee cannot again be called upon to bear the burden. [Para 19]

■

the provisions contained in sections 15,16 and 17. The deduction of tax may have to be made at the time of payment of salary but the calculation of the tax deductible will have to be made on the estimated salary income of the employee for the relevant financial ear according to the provision of the Act and the rules framed for this purpose. There is no warrant for the proposition that the amount of income-tax deductible will be calculated only on the amount that is actually handed over to the assessee. That apart, when an employer undertakes to pay tax-free income to an employee, what he undertakes is to pay an agreed sum of money plus the tax payable on that amount. The employee enjoys the benefit of the amount of tax which is paid on his account to the treasury. By this process, the employer discharges the statutory financial obligation of the employee. Therefore, the total salary of the employee must be the amount that is actually paid to him as also the amount of tax which was otherwise payable by him but which has been paid on his account by the company. Otherwise there will not be any difference between an amount of salary which is liable to be diminished by taxation and the same amount of salary which is paid free of tax. The burden of income-tax liability cannot be shifted by agreement. In the instant case, by undertaking to pay tax-free salary, the employer had really agreed to discharge the tax burden of the employee. The amount of tax that was paid by the employer was for and on behalf of the employee. Therefore, the amount of tax payable on the salary income of the employees, which was borne by the assessee, should be treated as part of the salary of the employee for the purpose of making estimate of income of the employee under section 192 and for the employer's failure to do so interest was rightly charged under section 201(1A ).

So far as the argument regarding the responsibility of the person handing overpayment was concerned, the person responsible for paying the salary of an employee is the employer himself. In the instant case, the company was the employer. It had to pay the salaries of its employees. An Officer or a clerk of the company might be engaged to actually hand over the pay cheque or the pay packet to the employees. But such payments were made for and on behalf of the company. The person responsible for payment of the salary was the employer itself. Thus, this argument of the assessee was to be rejected.

As regards the question of limitation, one of the consequences of failure to deduct or pay tax in accordance with the provisions of the Act is that the principal officer and the company shall be deemed to be an assessee in default in respect of the tax under the provisions of section 201. If an assessee is in default or deemed to be in default, the recovery of tax due might be made under the procedure specifically laid down for that purpose under the Act. The recovery could also be made by any other procedure. The period of limitation laid down by section 231 is confined to recovery proceedings under the Act. This provision of limitation could not curtail the power of the Government to file a suit to recover the outstanding amount of tax payable by any other process of law. The outstanding demand of tax could be recovered like any other debt due to the State. Even after the period of limitation laid down in section 231 is over, it is open to the Government to file a suit to recover the outstanding amount of tax subject to the provisions of Limitation Act. Therefore, in the instant case, it could not be said that the amount of tax deducted at source had become irrecoverable being barred by limitation.

On second appeal : HELD: It was quite evident from the TDS certificate dated 29-3-2004 issued by the deductors that the tax was actually deducted and paid into Government treasury only on 29-3-2004. From the record, it was found that the assessee had disclosed interest income receivable from two companies. However, during the years under consideration, the assessee neither actually received any interest, nor any certificate was given for deduction of tax at source. It appeared that there was some dispute between the assessee and its associates concerns to whom loans were given on interest. When the dispute was resolved, the tax was deducted at source for the period 1-4-2002 to 31-3-2003 on the amount credited to the assessee’s account; the tax so deducted was also deposited in the Government treasury on 29-3-2004 and a certificate dated 29-3-2004 was also issued to the assessee. As per the provisions of section 199, the credit for TDS has to be given in the assessment year in which the income relating to the tax deducted is assessed to tax. It also stipulates for giving credit to the assessee only on the production of certificate furnished under section 203. In the instant case, the TDS certificate furnished by the assessee clearly indicated that it pertained to the period 1-4-2002 to 31-3-2003 in respect of amount paid/credited, on which the deductors had deducted tax at source on 29-3-2004. Under the provisions of sections 194B, 199, 201, 203 and 205, a person responsible for making the payment to the assessee is under a statutory obligation to deduct tax at source and after deduction of the amount of tax, he is required to deposit the same to the credit of the Central Government and to issue a certificate of deduction. The assessee is entitled to claim credit for amount deducted at source only when the amount so deducted is found to be actually deposited to the credit of the Central Government and a certificate under section 203 is also furnished to this effect. Only on payment of amount to the credit of the Central Government, it would be treated as payment of tax. Accordingly, a mere claim of deduction of tax at source, or mere disclosing the respective income receivable in its books of account without any corresponding deduction of tax at source, would not entitle the assessee to claim credit of tax relatable to such income. So long as the amount deducted is not deposited in the coffers of the Central Government, there is no question of giving any credit for such amount of tax. But once tax is deducted on the income credited by the assessee in its books of account and a requisite certificate to this effect is issued by deductor after deposit of tax amount in the Government treasury, the assessee becomes entitled to the credit of such TDS, while computing the tax liability for the relevant period. [Para 5]

The scheme for giving credit for TDS has been modified through clauses 56 and 59 of the Finance Bill, 2002. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 201 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Consequences of failure to deduct or pay - Assessment year 1989-90 - Employee of assessee-company declared that he would be depositing certain amount in NSS - Assessee, on basis of computation submitted by employee, deducted tax at source - Employee did not deposit amount in NSS resulting in short deduction of tax at source - Whether assessee was duty bound to make enquiry and deduct tax at source and failure on part of assessee attracted provisions of section 201 and, therefore, interest was rightly levied - Held, yes - Whether in case employee had already deposited amount of short deducted tax no payment on account of tax short deducted at source would be required - Held, yes

FACT: On scrutiny of Form No. 24 filed by the assessee-company for the assessment year 1989-90, the Assessing Officer observed that net taxable salary of K, an employee of the assessee, was Rs. 54,240 whereon tax of Rs. 11,493 was to be deducted at source but the assessee had deducted only an amount of Rs. 9,000. The Assessing Officer, therefore, directed the assessee to pay an amount of Rs. 2,493 plus interest thereon and he also initiated penalty proceedings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the view of the Assessing Officer. The assessee’s case was that K had intimated the office that he would be depositing Rs. 20,000 in NSS as before but the assessee did not deposit the said amount and this misleading intimation resulted in short deduction of tax and there being no intentional default on the part of the assessee interest could not be levied on it and, further, since the employee had already paid short deducted tax, the assessee was not liable to make payment of short deducted tax.

HELD: It was not in dispute that the assessee deducted less tax by an amount of Rs. 2,493. The only defence advanced was that the assessee was misled by request of the concerned employee that he would be depositing Rs. 20,000 in NSS. It was the duty of the payer of remuneration to the employee to ensure that the employees would have deposited the impugned amount before the close of the financial years period within which tax was to be deducted at source. In case deposit of Rs. 20,000 was not made in time, the employer was duty bound to make enquiry and deduct tax at source. Thus, the provisions of section 201 were clearly attracted and interest had been properly levied. However, keeping in view the decision in Gwalior Rayon Silk Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1983] 140 ITR 832/ 14 Taxman 99 (MP), the employer is not responsible for making further payment of tax in case the same has already been paid by the concerned employee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was directed to verify as to whether ‘K’ had paid the amount of Rs. 2,493, i.e., short deduction of tax at source, and in case he had made the said payment, the assessee was to be allowed relief to the extent of Rs. 2,493. Payment of interest amounting to Rs. 1,277 was, however, sustained.

Section 199,  read with section 203, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment year 1997-98 - Whether once an employer has deducted tax at source, employee-assessee cannot be held responsible for payment once again and any such demand raised against employee-assessee cannot be recovered - Held, yes - In respect of relevant assessment year, assessee claimed credit of tax deducted at source (TDS) by his employer from salary paid to him - Assessee submitted that tax had been deducted by employer every time salary was paid to him but employer had not furnished Form No. 16 or any other relevant evidence to prove that tax had been deducted from salary paid to him - In support of his claim, assessee could furnish copies of pay slips only for two months and in respect of remaining 10 months, he did not furnish any documentary evidence and submitted that he was not in a position to procure said details and certificate from his employer - Assessing Officer held that in absence of statutory certificate, credit for TDS could not be given to assessee - Whether it was duty of Assessing Officer to collect details of payment made by employer of assessee and if it was found that tax had been deducted from salary paid to assessee, no recovery could be made from him and if Assessing Officer was able to obtain TDS certificate itself, then credit had to be given to assessment account of assessee - Held, yes - Whether matter was to be remitted back to Assessing Officer for proceeding further to collect said details - Held, yes

Section  199  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Credit for tax deducted  (Employees) - Assessment year  2012-13  - Assessee was an employee of Kingfisher Airlines - Kingfisher Airlines deducted TDS from salary paid to assessee and deposited same with Government - However, Assessing Officer disallowed credit of TDS to assessee on ground that Kingfisher Airlines did not deposit TDS with Government - Whether since assessee could not be blamed for non-deposit of TDS by Kingfisher Airlines, he could not be deprived of credit of TDS - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned order was to be set aside and credit of TDS was to be given to assessee - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]

Section 205 read with sections 234B and 234C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (General) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee, a salaried employee, filed his income tax return for assessment year 2013-14, reporting a gross salary from its employer-company with TDS deducted - However, a significant discrepancy was found between TDS amount deducted by employer and amount reflected in Form 26AS obtained from Income Tax Department website - Despite tax being deducted, a portion of amount had not been transmitted to Income Tax Department by employer - Consequently, assessee was deprived of receiving credit for full TDS amount, leading to a demand notice issued by income tax department, inclusive of interest under Sections 234B and 234C - Whether in case of an assessee whose tax has been deducted at source but not deposited to Government’s account by deductor, deductee-assessee shall not be called upon to pay demand to extent tax has been deducted from his income - Held, yes - Whether further, section 205 puts a bar on direct demand against assessee in such cases and demand on account of tax credit mismatch in such situations cannot be enforced coercively - Held, yes - Whether therefore, department should not deny benefit of tax deducted at source by employer during relevant financial years to assessee - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 15] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer had deducted tax at source from salary of assessee but had not deposited amount to Central Government’s account, in such case Assessing Officer could not deny benefit of tax deducted at source by employer to assessee and shall give credit of TDS amount to him

I. Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961  - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Credit for TDS) - Whether where assessee had followed regime framed in Act for collecting tax at source albeit through an agent of Government, i.e., deductor, and since agent/deductor failed to deposit tax with Government, recovery proceedings could only be initiated against agent/deductor and not against assessee/deductee; credit for TDS amount could not be denied to assessee - Held, yes [Para 21.2 and 3] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where deductor failed to deposit tax with Government, recovery proceedings could only be initiated against agent/deductor and not against assessee/deductee; credit for TDS amount could not be denied to assessee  INCOME TAX : Section 199 could not come in way of granting credit of TDS to deductee

Section 205, read with section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Illustrations) - Assessment years 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Assessee, a pilot by profession, was an employee of Kingfisher Airlines which had deducted tax at source from his salary but had not deposited amount to Central Government's account - Assessing Officer issued on assessee notice seeking recovery of outstanding demand - Whether in view of provisions of section 205 Assessing Officer shall not deny benefit of tax deducted at source by employer to assessee and shall give credit of TDS amount to him - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer deducted tax at source from assessee's salary but had not deposited amount with Central Govt. Assessing Officer would not deny benefit of tax deducted at source by employer to assessee

Section 205, read with sections 234B and 234BC, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (TDS Credit) - Assessment year 2024-25 - Assessee, an employee, received gross salary from his employer - Employer deducted TDS from his salary but did not issue Form 16 - Assessee filed return declaring salary and claimed said TDS credit - While processing return under section 143(1), CPC denied TDS credit on ground that no corresponding TDS was available in Form 26AS and assessee failed to submit Form 16 and levied interest under sections 234B and 234C - It was noted that employer had not paid any TDS after deducting from employee and after deducting TDS neither remitted amount to Government account nor filed any quarterly returns - Further assessee was an ex-employee and, thus, was not in a position to acquire relevant document from company - Whether since assessee had brought on record relevant salary slips to demonstrate that tax was deducted from salary, revenue could not deny tax credit to assessee - Held, yes - Whether, accordingly, interest levied under sections 234B and 234C was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee].

Section 205, read with sections 234B and 234BC, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (TDS Credit) - Assessment year 2024-25 - Assessee, an employee, received gross salary from his employer - Employer deducted TDS from his salary but did not issue Form 16 - Assessee filed return declaring salary and claimed said TDS credit - While processing return under section 143(1), CPC denied TDS credit on ground that no corresponding TDS was available in Form 26AS and assessee failed to submit Form 16 and levied interest under sections 234B and 234C - It was noted that employer had not paid any TDS after deducting from employee and after deducting TDS neither remitted amount to Government account nor filed any quarterly returns - Further assessee was an ex-employee and, thus, was not in a position to acquire relevant document from company - Whether since assessee had brought on record relevant salary slips to demonstrate that tax was deducted from salary, revenue could not deny tax credit to assessee - Held, yes - Whether, accordingly, interest levied under sections 234B and 234C was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer had not given any Form 16 to assessee after deducting TDS from salary and assessee had brought on record relevant salary slips to demonstrate that tax was deducted from salary, revenue could not deny tax credit to assessee

Section 205, read with section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Illustration) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee's employer deducted tax at source while making payment of wages but not deposited to Government Account - Assessing Officer did not grant credit of TDS which had been deducted from wages of assessee - Whether matter was to be restored back to file of Assessing Officer to verify fact and grant set off of tax deducted as well as reflected in salary slip and pass order afresh - Held, yes [Para 4] [Matter remanded]INCOME TAX : Where assessee's employer deducted tax at source while making payment of wages but not deposited to Government Account and Assessing Officer did not grant credit of TDS to assessee, matter was to be restored back to Assessing Officer to verify fact and grant set off of tax deducted

Section 205 read with sections 234B and 234C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (General) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee, a salaried employee, filed his income tax return for assessment year 2013-14, reporting a gross salary from its employer-company with TDS deducted - However, a significant discrepancy was found between TDS amount deducted by employer and amount reflected in Form 26AS obtained from Income Tax Department website - Despite tax being deducted, a portion of amount had not been transmitted to Income Tax Department by employer - Consequently, assessee was deprived of receiving credit for full TDS amount, leading to a demand notice issued by income tax department, inclusive of interest under Sections 234B and 234C - Whether in case of an assessee whose tax has been deducted at source but not deposited to Government’s account by deductor, deductee-assessee shall not be called upon to pay demand to extent tax has been deducted from his income - Held, yes - Whether further, section 205 puts a bar on direct demand against assessee in such cases and demand on account of tax credit mismatch in such situations cannot be enforced coercively - Held, yes - Whether therefore, department should not deny benefit of tax deducted at source by employer during relevant financial years to assessee - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 15] [In favour of assessee]

Section 199, read with sections 234B and 234C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Illustrations) - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - During year under consideration, assessee had earned salary income - It had claimed refund of TDS deducted under section 192 - Assessing Officer denied claim of TDS to assessee on ground that same was not reflecting in Form 26AS and consequently, had charged interest under sections 234B and 234C - Whether since assessee himself acting as MD and CEO of its company did not deduct TDS on salary paid/payable to himself for working as MD and CEO of company, he could not be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong and, thus, was not entitled to any claim of set-off of TDS, which was never deposited by company - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 13] [In favour of revenue]

Section 199, read with sections 234B and 234C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Illustrations) - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - During year under consideration, assessee had earned salary income - It had claimed refund of TDS deducted under section 192 - Assessing Officer denied claim of TDS to assessee on ground that same was not reflecting in Form 26AS and consequently, had charged interest under sections 234B and 234C - Whether since assessee himself acting as MD and CEO of its company did not deduct TDS on salary paid/payable to himself for working as MD and CEO of company, he could not be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong and, thus, was not entitled to any claim of set-off of TDS, which was never deposited by company - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 13] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee being managing director and chief executive officer of company himself did not deduct TDS on salary paid/payable to himself for working as MD and CEO of company, he could not be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong and, thus, was not entitled to any claim of set off of TDS which was never deposited by company

I. Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961  - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Credit for TDS) - Whether where assessee had followed regime framed in Act for collecting tax at source albeit through an agent of Government, i.e., deductor, and since agent/deductor failed to deposit tax with Government, recovery proceedings could only be initiated against agent/deductor and not against assessee/deductee; credit for TDS amount could not be denied to assessee - Held, yes [Para 21.2 and 3] [In favour of assessee]  II. Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961  - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (General) - Whether section 199 could not come in way of granting credit of TDS to deductee - Held, yes [Para 28] [In favour of assessee]

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Tax deducted at source) - Assessment years  2009-10  and 2011-12 - Assessee was employed with company KIL - During course of employment, KIL deducted TDS from assessee's salary but, KIL did not deposit same with Income-tax authorities - Accordingly, revenue raised demand against assessee - Assessee claimed that TDS was duly reflected in Form 16A issued by KIL and, thus, he was not liable to pay tax - Whether in view of decision in case of Sanjay Sudan v. Asstt. CIT [2023] 148 taxmann.com 329/292 Taxman 138/452 ITR 107 (Delhi), revenue could not recover TDS from assessee - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]

Section 205, read with section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Illustration) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee's employer deducted tax at source while making payment of wages but not deposited to Government Account - Assessing Officer did not grant credit of TDS which had been deducted from wages of assessee - Whether matter was to be restored back to file of Assessing Officer to verify fact and grant set off of tax deducted as well as reflected in salary slip and pass order afresh - Held, yes [Para 4] [Matter remanded]

Section  205,  read with section  199,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee  (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year  2020-21 and 2021-22  - Assessee’s employer deducted tax at source from salary but failed to deposit same with Government - While processing return, Assessing Officer denied credit of such TDS to assessee due to system mismatch and raised demand - High Court held that in view of section 205 read with CBDT  Instruction No. 275 dated 1-6-2015  and Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016, no demand could be raised against assessee where tax had been deducted but not deposited by the deductor - High Court further directed CBDT to modify software so that no demand could be raised in future in cases where there would be mismatch between TDS and tax not deposited by deductor in case of deductee - Whether since aforesaid directions had nothing to do with case on merits and would not affect assessee, direction issued for changes to be made in software were to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 5] [Partly in favour of revenue]

Section 201 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Consequence of failure to deduct or pay - Where employer of assessee paid TDS on perquisite value of stock options allotted to its employees which was subsequently recovered from respective employees, but later on, such deduction of tax was held to be not in accordance with law, employees were entitled to refund of amount of tax, even though there was delay in filing return [In favour of assessee]

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year 2020-21 and 2021-22 - Employer of assessee deducted tax at source from salary income of assessee for two years but did not deposit same with Government - When assessee filed return of income disclosing tax deducted at source, there was a mismatch in system and accordingly, demand was raised upon assessee by an intimation issued under section 143(1) - Whether since there was failure on part of employer to deposit tax deducted at source from salary income of assessee, revenue could not have raised any demand against assessee in view of provisions of section 205 read with Instruction No. 275 dated 01.06.2015 and Office Memorandum dated 11.03.2016 - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 10] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Instruction No. 275, dated 1-6-2015 and Office Memorandum F. No. 275/29/2014-IT(B), dated 11-3-2016.

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year 2020-21 and 2021-22 - Employer of assessee deducted tax at source from salary income of assessee for two years but did not deposit same with Government - When assessee filed return of income disclosing tax deducted at source, there was a mismatch in system and accordingly, demand was raised upon assessee by an intimation issued under section 143(1) - Whether since there was failure on part of employer to deposit tax deducted at source from salary income of assessee, revenue could not have raised any demand against assessee in view of provisions of section 205 read with Instruction No. 275 dated 01.06.2015 and Office Memorandum dated 11.03.2016 - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 10] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer of assessee deducted tax at source from salary income of assessee but did not deposit same with Government, Assessing Officer could not have raised any demand against assessee in view of provisions of section 205 read with CBDT's Instruction No. 275 dated 1-6-2015

Section  199,  read with section  205,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Credit for tax deducted  (Scope of provision) - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessee let out his flat to a company under a leave and license agreement - Licensee deducted TDS from rent receipts but did not deposit part of it - Assessing Officer declined TDS credit to assessee to extent of shortfall on ground that same was not reflected in Form 26AS - It was noted that assessee had submitted necessary evidence like copies of ITR, computation, statement in Form 26AS, leave and license agreement, bank statement to support facts of case - Furthermore, revenue had not doubted fact that tax was deducted at source but was not deposited by deductor - Whether thus, Assessing Officer was directed to allow credit of TDS after due verification of facts on record - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment year 2006-07 - Assessee was a judicial officer in State Judicial Service - For relevant assessment year, he claimed credit for tax deducted at source by employer - He also furnished form 16 but as it was self attested instead of being attested by employer, Assessing Officer did not give credit for tax deducted at source - Whether a complete machinery is provided under Act for recovery of tax deducted at source from person who has deducted such tax at source and revenue is barred from recovering such amount from person from whose income tax had been deducted at source - Held, yes - Whether assessee was a Judicial Officer in State Judicial Service and if tax was deducted at source it was most unlikely that it had not been deposited in treasury by State Government - Held, yes - Whether therefore impugned order was to be set aside and Assessing Officer was to be directed to  verify as to whether as a matter of fact, tax was deducted at source from salary of assessee and if that was so found to be correct, to grant further credit for tax, as the case may be - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

Section 205, read with  section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Scope of provision) - Assessment years 2009-10, 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Employer paid salary to assessee after deduction of tax at source but did not deposit same with department - Assessing Officer did not allow credit of tax deducted at source and raised demand against assessee towards tax and interest - Whether assessee having accepted salary after deduction of tax at source had no further control over it and it was duty of employer to pay deducted tax to department and employer having failed to perform his duty to deposit deducted tax, assessee could not be penalized - Held, yes - Whether section 199 could not operate as impediment to grant relief to assessee and, thus, impugned demand deserved to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Instruction No. 275, dated 1-6-2015; Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016 and Press Release, dated 11-3-2016

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at 
source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment year 2002-03 - Assessee derived salary income from one company and professional fees from another company but those employers did not issue any tax deducted at source (TDS) certificates to assessee - However, he filed his return claiming credit of said TDS, which was disallowed by Assessing Officer - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) could not grant relief to 
assessee on ground that he could not produce evidence of TDS deduction except bank statements and some pay-slips - However, 
 Commissioner (Appeals) directed Assessing Officer to give full credit of said TDS in case, it was established on verification from TDS wing that payers actually deducted tax and filed TDS return - Whether there was no error in direction of Commissioner (Appeals) under given facts and circumstances of case - Held, yes

Section 220 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection  recovery of tax - When assessee deemed in default - Where Assessing Officer passed order under section 254/143(3) to give effect to order of Tribunal assessing interest income in assessment year 1993-94 but committed a mistake in allowing credit of TDS in assessment year 1992-93 and, therefore, a rectification was made to withdraw credit for TDS for 1992-93 and give credit for such TDS for year 1993-94, interest could not be charged for withdrawal of TDS.

Section 205, read with  section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Scope of provision) - Assessment years 2009-10, 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Employer paid salary to assessee after deduction of tax at source but did not deposit same with department - Assessing Officer did not allow credit of tax deducted at source and raised demand against assessee towards tax and interest - Whether assessee having accepted salary after deduction of tax at source had no further control over it and it was duty of employer to pay deducted tax to department and employer having failed to perform his duty to deposit deducted tax, assessee could not be penalized - Held, yes - Whether section 199 could not operate as impediment to grant relief to assessee and, thus, impugned demand deserved to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer paid salary to assessee after deduction of tax at source but employer did not deposit same with department, assessee could not be penalized for failure of employer to perform his duty to deposit deducted tax

Section 201 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Consequences of failure to deduct or pay - Assessment year 1989-90 - Employee of assessee-company declared that he would be depositing certain amount in NSS - Assessee, on basis of computation submitted by employee, deducted tax at source - Employee did not deposit amount in NSS resulting in short deduction of tax at source - Whether assessee was duty bound to make enquiry and deduct tax at source and failure on part of assessee attracted provisions of section 201 and, therefore, interest was rightly levied - Held, yes - Whether in case employee had already deposited amount of short deducted tax no payment on account of tax short deducted at source would be required - Held, yes

Section 201 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Consequence of failure to deduct or pay - Assessment years 2001-02 to 2004-05 - Whether it is only where deductee's tax liability had already been determined following prescribed procedure and found payable upon considering payment under section 140A that TDS to that extent, could be collected or recovered by revenue from deductor, i.e., at any time, adjusting same against deductee's tax liability - Held, yes - Whether however, where there is no such outstanding demand, i.e., of determined tax liability of deductee, it is not possible to subscribe to view that TDS could be collected or recovered at any time, i.e., without any time limitation; in such case recovery would be subject to it being initiated within a reasonable period which is a period up to which tax could be assessed in hands of deductee - Held, yes [Paras 4 and 5] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where deductor fails to deduct tax at source and there is no determined tax liability of deductee, TDS can be recovered from deductor only within period up to which tax could be assessed in hands of deductee
Identification of employee is therefore held to be must before effecting such recovery.

Section 199, read with sections 143(1), 209 and 234B, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Conditions precedent) - Assessment year 2019-20 - Whether credit for amount of tax deducted at source is not dependent upon its subsequent deposit by deductor, hence, requirement for allowing credit is only of amount of tax deducted at source and not amount eventually getting deposited with Government after deduction - Held, yes - Whether section 234B provides that where an assessee fails to pay due advance tax computed as per section 209, he shall be liable to pay simple interest at specified rate on amount of assessed tax - Held, yes - Whether where there is an income on which tax is deductible at source, then such income will be reduced for determining advance tax liability and consequential interest liability under section 234B, even if no tax was actually deducted at source - Held, yes - Whether Finance Act, 2012 inserted a proviso to section 209(1) nullifying above position of deducting income on which tax is deductible but not actually deducted - Held, yes - Whether thus, where a sum of Rs. 8.21 lakhs was duly deducted at source by employer from salaries credited/paid to assessee for year under consideration, benefit of such tax deducted at source had to be allowed in intimation under section 143(1), notwithstanding fact that it was not deposited - Held, yes [Paras 7, 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where a sum was duly deducted at source by employer from salaries credited/paid to assessee for year under consideration, benefit of such tax deducted at source had to be allowed in intimation under section 143(1), notwithstanding fact that it was not deposited

I. Section 36(1)(va), read with  section 43B, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Employee's contributions (PF/ESI) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Whether deduction under section 36(1)(va) could not be allowed where amount collected towards employees’ contribution to PF/ESI was deposited beyond due date prescribed under relevant Act even if such contribution was deposited within due date of filing of return - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of revenue]  II. Section 37(1), read with  section 201, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowablilty of (Interest on delayed payment of TDS) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee had claimed a sum as expenses for interest paid on TDS - Assessing Officer observed that such payment of interest on delayed deposit of TDS was not an allowable deduction and accordingly disallowed aforesaid expenditure claimed by assessee – It was found that TDS by deeming fiction has been made tax liability of deductor to ensure that recipient of payment cannot fade away without paying due taxes on income part of such receipts - Once, deductee pays due taxes, deductor is absolved from said tax liability but not of interest liability on delayed payment - Allowing of such interest payment on delayed deposit of TDS as deduction would defeat very purpose of TDS provisions ensuring deduction of taxes from income of recipient and payment/deposit thereof with Central Government within due time - Whether therefore, interest payment on delayed deposit of Income-tax, whether TDS or otherwise, was not an allowable expenditure - Held, yes [Paras 24 and 25] [In favour of revenue]

Section 205, read with sections 192, 199 and 203, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection and recovery of tax - Bar against direct demand on assessee - Assessment year 1996-97 - Whether in view of section 205, income-tax authorities, under no circumstances, can make assessee liable to make payment of any tax to extent to which tax has been deducted at source by person paying salary to assessee under section 192 - Held, yes - Whether, however, at same time, credit for tax deducted at source cannot be given to assessee unless he submits certificate as prescribed under section 203 in 
 respect of TDS as per provisions of section 199 - Held, yes - Whether till powers available to income-tax authorities to enforce payment of tax by deductor and also enforce issue of certificate in respect thereof to payee were not exercised by revenue authorities to corner deductor of tax, no tax as well as interest pertaining thereto could be recovered from assessee - Held, yes.

Section 199, read with section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Credit of TDS) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was an employee of Indian Railways - He had received salary income but had not filed his return of income - Accordingly, Assessing Officer passed an assessment order under section 144 and made addition to assessee's income based on salary received by assessee as reflected in Form 26AS - Assessee contended that TDS was deducted from his salary which was duly reflected in Form 26AS, therefore, matter should be remanded back to Assessing Officer for verification of facts and to allow credit of TDS - It was noted that addition in case of assessee was made by Assessing Officer based on income of assessee reflected in Form 26AS, but TDS credit available in Form 26AS was not allowed to assessee - Whether since legitimate credit of TDS was not allowed by Assessing Officer, in spite of having such facts on records, there was perversity in order of Assessing Officer and therefore, matter was to be remanded back to Assessing Officer for fresh adjudication - Held, yes [Para 8] [Matter remanded]

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment year 2003-04 - Whether when a particular income is received by assessee after deduction of tax at source and said TDS has been duly deposited with Government and assessee has received requisite certificate to this effect, then on production of said certificate assessee becomes entitled to credit of TDS, even if assessee has not directly offered said income for tax as assessee considers that same is not liable for tax - Held, yes

Undisputedly, within the period as provided under the law and as directed by the Commissioner, Provident Funds, the petitioner made deposits with the department. So far as the question of recovery of the contribution of the employees was concerned, everybody knows that it would always be a herculean task to recover money from an employee which he has already pocketed. The amount could only be recovered from the future salary or could be received if employees were ready and willing to make deposits.

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Illustrations) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Whether as per section 205 read with instruction No. 275/29/2014, dated 1-6-2015, assessee cannot be called upon to pay tax, which has been deducted at source from his income; since Act places a bar on a direct demand qua deductee assessee, same cannot be enforced coercively - Held, yes - For assessment year 2012-13, assessee's employer, i.e., KAL, had withheld tax payable on salary of assessee - KAL did not deposit withholding tax and, hence, a demand was raised by revenue - According to assessee, because of said outstanding demand, refund payable to assessee for assessment year 2015-16 was not paid to him, and instead, refund was set-off against said demand - Whether since demand qua tax withheld by employer could not be recovered from assessee nor same amount could be adjusted against future refund, if any, payable to him, adjustment of demand against future refund amounted to an indirect recovery of tax, which was barred under section 205 and, thus, revenue was not entitled in law to adjust said demand - Held, yes [Paras 9 and 12] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Revenue cannot adjust withheld tax which has not been deposited by deductor/employer in Central Government Account, against refund due and payable to assessee-employee

I. Section 36(1)(va), read with  section 43B, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Employee's contributions (PF/ESI) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Whether deduction under section 36(1)(va) could not be allowed where amount collected towards employees’ contribution to PF/ESI was deposited beyond due date prescribed under relevant Act even if such contribution was deposited within due date of filing of return - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Deduction under section 36(1)(va) could not be allowed where amount collected towards employees’ contribution to PF/ESI was deposited beyond due date prescribed under relevant Act even if such contribution was deposited within due date of filing of return  INCOME TAX : Interest payment on delayed deposit of Income-tax, whether TDS or otherwise, is not an allowable expenditure

I. Section  199,  read with section  205,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Credit for tax deducted  (Scope of) - Assessment year  2022-23  - Assessee, a law firm, received payments from its clients net of TDS, i.e., deductors withheld applicable TDS before releasing amounts - Assessee claimed credit of TDS while offering entire gross receipts to tax - However, Assessing Officer denied claim solely on ground that such amounts did not feature in Form No. 26AS - Consequently, a demand was raised comprising disallowed TDS together with interest under sections 234B and 234C - It was noted that assessee had demonstrated deduction of tax at source through its invoices and bank statements - Reconciliation placed on record showed deduction by a company which was not deposited owing to company's financial condition - Whether section 205 erects a clear bar against making a direct demand on assessee to extent tax had been deducted at source from his income and moment deduction was shown on strength of primary evidence, embargo of section 205 attaches and deductee could not again be called upon to bear burden - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had already brought corresponding income to tax, denial of credit in assessee's hands, because deductor failed to deposit or misreported deduction, would result in taxing same income twice - Held, yes - Whether thus, assessee was entitled to credit of TDS to extent deduction from its receipts was established on basis of contemporaneous material placed on record - Held, yes [Paras 19, 24 and 27] [In favour of assessee]

Section 199, read with section 205, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Conditions precedent) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessing Officer disallowed claim made by assessee for credit of TDS for assessment year 2005-06 on ground that payment was made by customer in assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08 - Assessee submitted that income in respect of which TDS credit was not allowed, was shown in assessment year 2005-06 on accrual basis on raising invoices of customer NHPC but customer NHPC withheld payments - Payment was made and TDS was deposited in subsequent years - Whether in view of provisions of section 199 and on basis of various judicial ruling, it was to be held that tax deducted at source but not paid to Central Government within financial year could not be treated as payment of tax on behalf of assessee - Held, yes - Whether since TDS was actually deducted and deposited into Government account in financial years 2005-06 and 2006-07, credit of same was allowable in corresponding assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08 and not in assessment year 2005-06 - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of revenue]IT : Tax deducted at source by deductor but not paid to Central Government within financial year could not be treated as payment of tax on behalf of assessee deductee and thus, assessee, could not claim credit of TDS in that financial year

Section  205  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee  (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year  2020-21 and 2021-22  - Employer of assessee deducted tax at source from salary income of assessee for two years but did not deposit same with Government - When assessee filed return of income disclosing tax deducted at source, there was a mismatch in system and accordingly, demand was raised upon assessee by an intimation issued under section 143(1) - High Court held that since there was failure on part of employer to deposit tax deducted at source from salary income of assessee, revenue could not have raised any demand against assessee in view of provisions of section 205 read with  Instruction No. 275 dated 01.06.2015  and Office Memorandum dated 11.03.2016 - It was noted that common order passed by High Court had already been considered in a connected matter in Income-tax Assessing Officer, Baroda v. Shobhan Shantilal Doshi [2026] 182 taxmann.com 555 (SC), and same was disposed of by clarifying directions given with reference to changes to be made in software - Whether in view of directions already issued, no further order was required to be passed in impugned petition and, thus, SLP was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 3 and 4] [In favour of assessee]

facts.text:
■

The assessee, an employee, received salary on which TDS was deducted. However, the employer had not deposited the TDS to the account of the Central Government.

■

The assessee had filed his return of income and claimed credit of the TDS that was deducted in the salary.

■

In the intimation issued, the credit of the TDS had not been granted and a demand was raised against the assessee in lieu of the credit of the TDS not granted.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee was an employee of company, D. The employer had deducted TDS from monthly salary of the assessee, however, same was not deposited to the Government. The assessee filed return and claimed TDS as pre-paid taxes.

■

The Assessing Officer denied assessee's claim.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) restored the matter back to the file of the Assessing Officer directing him to verify the claim of the assessee from Form 26AS and ITR and if the claim was found to be correct, an appropriate amount of TDS credit be allowed to the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee–employee filed a return declaring total income of about Rs. 70.37 lakhs for the year under consideration and claimed TDS credit of about Rs. 18.10 lakhs.

■

The return was processed under section 143(1) by CPC, which allowed TDS credit of about Rs. 0.60 lakhs only, restricting the balance claim.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the AO to grant an opportunity of being heard, verify the TDS with Form 26AS and other relevant material to ascertain whether it related to the income offered in the year, and thereafter grant credit if the claim was found correct.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee contended that his employer had paid salary of about Rs. 57.50 lakhs and deducted TDS of about Rs. 17.50 lakhs for which credit should be allowed; the Revenue contended the employer had not deposited the deducted TDS in the Government account and, therefore, credit could not be allowed.

The petitioner-assessee was a pilot by profession and was an employee of 'K' Airlines. The Airlines deducted TDS in case of assessee, however, since amount had not been deposited by the Airlines in the Central Government Account, the credit when claimed by the assessee was not given by the respondent and the demand had been raised with interest.

The assessee filed rectification applications under section 154 and asked for cancellation of demand. These were ignored and recovery notice was issued to assessee by respondent Income-tax Department.

On writ petition under article 226:

■

The assessee, employee, received salary after deduction of tax at source. The assessee was also issued TDS Form showing full amount of Tax Deducted at source. However, the employer company had gone into liquidation and consequently, the tax deducted was not deposited in Government account.

■

The assessee filed return claiming TDS credit.

■

The Assessing Officer raised demand onaccount of denial of TDS credit due to the mismatch with Form 26AS.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessment order.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee, a salaried employee, filed his income tax return for assessment year 2013-14, reporting a gross salary from its employer-company with TDS deducted. However, a significant discrepancy was found between the TDS amount deducted by the employer and the amount reflected in Form 26AS obtained from the Income Tax Department website.

■

Despite the tax being deducted, a portion of the amount had not been transmitted to the Income Tax Department by the employer.

■

Consequently, the assessee was deprived of receiving credit for the full TDS amount, leading to a demand notice issued by the income tax department, inclusive of interest under Sections 234B and 234C.

■

In the instant writ petition, the assessee argued that they should not be penalized for the employer's failure to fulfill this obligation. They relied on section 205, which prohibitted direct demands on the assessee, and cited circulars dated 01.06.2015 issued CBDT to support their argument.

■

The assessee-pilot by profession, was an employee of Kingfisher Airlines. During the relevant assessment years, Kingfisher Airlines (deductor) had deducted TDS on assessee's salary but the same was not deposited by the deductor in the Central Government Account.

■

The assessee filed return and claimed credit for TDS.

■

However, the Assessing Officer did not grant credit due to mismatch of TDS and raised demand along with interest.

■

Thereafter, the assessee received intimation under Section 245 proposing adjustment of refund against the outstanding demand.

■

On writ :

Since 16-4-2008, the assessee was employed with Kingfisher Airlines Limited as an airlines pilot at the rank of Captain.

For the relevant assessment years the employer paid salary to the assessee after deduction of tax at source but did not deposit the same with the department.

The Assessing Officer processed under section 143(1) the return of income furnished by the assessee and did not allow the credit of tax deducted at source and raised demand against him towards tax and interest.

On writ petition :

The assessee derived salary income from a company for which he worked from October 2000 to January 2002 and also received professional fees from another company. Since assessee’s employers deducted tax at source (TDS), from such payment made by them, he claimed credit thereof in his return accordingly. The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the same on the ground that the assessee did not possess the requisite TDS certificate. On appeal, since the assessee could not produce the evidence of TDS deduction except the bank statements and some payslips, the Commissioner (Appeals) could not grant relief to the assessee. He, however, directed the Assessing Officer to verify from the TDS wing to establish whether the payers actually deducted the tax and/or filed the TDS return or not. He was also directed to give full credit of the TDS made on the basis of such verification report in case the same was found positive. The Commissioner (Appeals) alternatively directed the Assessing Officer that in case, the credit for TDS could not be made, at least the corresponding receipts should be reduced so that only the net receipts credited in the bank account be treated as the gross receipts on which the assessee might agree to pay the taxes again.

On cross appeal :

■

The assessee was an employee of Kingfisher Airlines.

■

Kingfisher Airlines deducted TDS from salary of assessee but did not deposit same with Government.

■

The Assessing Officer disallowed the amount of TDS and raised a demand against the assessee.

■

On writ petition, the assessee contended that the respondent had recovered the substantial amount of said demand from the amount of refund which became due to the assessee.

■
