The assessee-employee filed its return claiming TDS amounting to Rs.10.45 lakhs which was deducted by employer from salary under section 192,

■

The Assessing Officer denied claim on the ground that the employer of the assessee had not reflected the TDS in Form No. 26AS.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

The assessee’s employer paid salary to him after deducting the tax therefrom. But despite repeated requests made by the assessee, his employer did not furnish the requisite TDS certificate. Consequently, he filed his return without Form No. 16 and also requested the Assessing Officer to enforce the issue of said certificate by the employer in exercise of his jurisdiction over the matter. However, in the absence of the same, the Assessing Officer framed the assessment under section 143(1)(a) raising tax demand in respect of salary income which was levied for the TDS certificate not furnished as well as interest payable in respect of the said tax. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that in the absence of Form No. 16 and Form No. 24, giving credit for TDS on salary did not appear to be justified, though the assessee could not be asked to pay the tax again to the extent to which tax had already been deducted in view of section 205. He, accordingly, directed the Assessing Officer to ask the assessee to obtain the same from the employer and furnish the same.

On second appeal :

■

The assessee was employed with TLPL. The employer i.e. TLPL had paid gross salary to the assessee during the year April 2023 to August 23 and deducted TDS under section 192 but the TLPL did not provide any Form 16 to the assessee for the same period.

■

The assessee declared the gross salary income for filing the return of income and claimed the above said TDS. While processing the return under section 143(1), since there was no TDS credit against the above said salary, the TDS was denied to the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee by observing that the assessee had not submitted Form 16 issued by the employer and the same was also not reflected in Form 26AS.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

For the assessment year 2004-05 the assessee-company had paid salary of certain sum to its non-resident employees and claimed deduction of same under section 40(a)( iii). During the course of the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer asked the assessee as to why the expenditure on account of salary be not disallowed under section 40(a)( iii). The assessee submitted before the Assessing Officer that since tax had already been paid to the credit of the Government account, no such disallowance was called for, as section 40(a)( iii) does not intend so. However, the Assessing Officer after making a reference to the provision contained in section 40(a)(iii ), and to the Circular No. 7 of 2003, dated 5-9-2003 issued by the CBDT, had taken the view that it was obligatory on the part of the assessee-company to deposit the TDS deducted on payment of salary, to the credit of the Government account by 7-4-2004, as provided under rule 30 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and since TDS on salary was not paid within the prescribed time, such expenditure was not allowable under section 40(a)(iii ). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to allow the deduction inasmuch as disallowance could be made only when tax had not been paid nor had not been deducted.

On revenue's appeal :

■

The assessees were salaried employees of ASPL. Tax at source (TDS) was deducted from their salaries but was not remitted by the employer to the Income Tax Department.

■

Due to such non-remittance, the assessee’s faced tax demands.

■

In the instant writ, the assessees contended that they should not be liable for TDS not deposited by the employer.

■

The assessee had let out his ownership flat to a company under a leave and license agreement. The assessee received the license fee after deduction of the tax from licensee. The licensee had deducted TDS of Rs. 1.48 lakhs but deposited only about Rs. 0.36 lakhs.

■

The Assessing Officer declined TDS credit to assessee to the extent of the shortfall of Rs. 1.12 lakhs on ground that samewas not reflected in Form 26AS.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the claim of assessee, stating that the dispute needed to be settled between the Licensee and Licensor, thus the assessee was liable to pay legitimate taxes even if it was on account of failure of the deductor / licensee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee-company employed a Canadian national 'G' at a fixed remuneration with the perquisites of rent-free accommodation, car with driver and a servant. 'G' filed his tax return and paid taxes after self-assessment. The Assessing Officer noticed from a perusal of the bank account of the employee and the TDS return filed by the assessee that no salary had been paid to the employee nor any deduction under section 192 made by the assessee. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, held that the assessee was in default under sections 201 and 201(1A). Consequently, the Assessing Officer determined the liability arising on account of interest. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had paid the salary to 'G', the expatriate employee through its partner abroad but subsequently when the revenue started surveys, the assessee in an attempt to get out of the mess took the plea that it had not made any such payment and that no tax at source was deductible. The Commissioner, therefore, directed the Assessing Officer to give credit to the taxes paid by 'G' and recover the remaining account including interest from the assessee. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the obligation to deduct tax at source did not arise as the salary payable to 'G' had not been actually paid to him and, therefore, the assessee was not liable to either pay tax under section 201 or interest under section 201(1A).

On appeal :

For short deduction of tax at source from salaries paid to employees, the ITO levied interest on the assessee from the date of default to the date of payment, but the Commissioner (Appeals) held that interest was chargeable only up to the date of expiry of the limitation period prescribed for com-mencing recovery proceedings in section 231.

On second appeal :

■

The petitioners/assessees were employees of respondent no.2. They were being paid monthly emoluments/salary, after deduction of TDS (taxes at source) by respondent No.2. Since the year 2019, respondent No.2 was involved in criminal proceedings initiated against it by the Enforcement Directorate (ED), in regard to the financial crimes. There was an investigation undertaken by SEBI on investors grievances in relation to violation of the securities law. During the course of such investigation, the directors of respondent no.2 as also some senior officers of respondent no.2 were arrested. As a consequence of these irregularities, there were defaults on the part of respondent no.2 in the payment of petitioners’ salary. Some of the employees did not at all receive their salaries while some others received delayed payments. Subsequently, the petitioners received from department the impugned notices demanding payment of income tax alongwith interest, on account of non-deposit of TDS amount by respondent no.2, which according to the petitioners, were shown to have been deducted from the salary slips as issued to the petitioners.

■

In instant writ petition to the High Court the petitioners contended that it was not permissible for department to issue such demand notices against the petitioners in view of clear provisions of section 205 of the Income Tax Act, which bars any demand against the assessees. The provision ordained that where tax is deductible at source under the provisions of Chapter XVII, the assessee should not be called upon to pay tax himself to the extent to which the tax had been deducted from the income. In this view of the matter, the petitioners submitted that no demand could had been foisted by department on the petitioners. To this effect, the petitioners had also made representations on the portal of the department that the demand might be withdrawn. However, the same had not been acted upon and the demand was stated to have subsisted.

■

The assessee was an ex-employee of company KSBL. The employer of assessee deducted tax from salary of the assessee but not deposited same with the Government. Accordingly, the assessee was subjected to assessment without giving the set off of the tax deducted from its salary and demand was raised upon the assessee by an intimation issued under section 143(1).

■

On writ petition :

■

The assessee, law firm, was engaged in providing legal services. The assessee received payments from clients which were net of tax deducted at source, the deductors having withheld the applicable TDS before releasing amounts. The assessee while filing return claimed credit for such deductions while offering the entire gross receipts to tax.

■

The Assessing Officer denied credit of TDS solely on the ground that such amounts did not feature in Form No. 26AS. Consequently, a demand was raised comprising the disallowed TDS together with interest under section 234B and under section 234C.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the denial of credit, holding that unless the deduction appeared in Form 26AS, the assessee could not be allowed relief. As regards levy of interest under sections 234B and 234C, the Commissioner (Appeals) held the same to be consequential and mandatory.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee was employed by 'K' Airlines Limited as a pilot from November 2008 to July 2010. During the financial years 2008-09 and 2010-11, the employer deducted tax at source out of the salary of the assessee but failed to deposit the same with the Income-tax Authorities.

■

The assessee filed return of income for assessment year 2009-10 declaring its income claiming the credit of TDS which the employer deducted from the salary. However, since the employer did not deposit the same with Income-tax Authorities, the return of income filed by the assessee was processed under section 143(1) by Jurisdictional Assessing Officer without giving credit for the same and raising demand of Rs. 11.42 lakhs.

■

The assessee filed return of income for subsequent period and the same were processed under section 143(1). In the event of the refund due to the assessee, the same was adjusted against the demand of assessment years 2009-10 or 2010-11.

■

Meanwhile the assessee filed an application for rectification under section 154 against the demand raised in the intimation for assessment year 2009-10 and adjustment of refunds of subsequent years. The Jurisdictional Assessing Officer passed an order rejecting the rectification application which was assailed before Commissioner (Appeals) who directed the Jurisdictional Assessing Officer to rectify the mistake apparent on record by verifying the contention of the assessee.

■

For long time, no order giving effect to the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was passed. The assessee thereafter requested the Jurisdictional Assessing Officer to give appeal effect of the said order.

■

Thereafter, the assessee received intimation under section 245 via E-mail proposing to adjust the refund of assessment year 2023-24 against the outstanding demand of assessment years 2009-10 and 2011-12.

■

On writ:

For the assessment years 1968-69 to 1970-71, the assessee-company deducted tax at source from salaries of its employees but failed to pay the same to the credit of the Central Government as required under section 200, read with rule 30, of the Income-tax Rules, 1962. The reason given by the assessee-company was that it faced stringent financial problems on account of several reasons which were beyond its control. The ITO treated the assessee company as in default and charged interest under section 201(1A). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), however, deleted the interest on the ground that the proceedings for recovery of tax deducted at source were barred by limitation under section 231.

On appeal by the revenue:

Facts

During proceedings under section 143(1) it was noticed that the amount which had been collected by the assessee from its employees as their contribution towards ESI and Provident Fund had not been deposited by the due date prescribed under the Employees State Insurance and PF Acts.

The Assessing Officer disallowed the said payments holding that the assessee was not entitled to deduction of the said amount in view of section 36(1)(va), read with section 43B.

The Commissioner as well as the Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee.

Revenue's contentions

The employer can get deduction of the contribution made by him even if it is not deposited within the time granted under the Employees Welfare Funds Acts in case the said amounts are deposited by the assessee/employer before or at the time of filing of the returns. However, as far as the employees contribution is concerned then the assessee cannot get benefit of deduction even if amount is deposited before filing of the return.

Issue involved

Whether where amount was not deposited by due date under welfare Acts employer-assessee could also take the benefit of deduction of contributions which was collected from its employees if the same was paid before furnishing of return?

On scrutiny of Form No. 24 filed by the assessee-company for the assessment year 1989-90, the Assessing Officer observed that net taxable salary of K, an employee of the assessee, was Rs. 54,240 whereon tax of Rs. 11,493 was to be deducted at source but the assessee had deducted only an amount of Rs. 9,000. The Assessing Officer, therefore, directed the assessee to pay an amount of Rs. 2,493 plus interest thereon and he also initiated penalty proceedings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the view of the Assessing Officer. The assessee’s case was that K had intimated the office that he would be depositing Rs. 20,000 in NSS as before but the assessee did not deposit the said amount and this misleading intimation resulted in short deduction of tax and there being no intentional default on the part of the assessee interest could not be levied on it and, further, since the employee had already paid short deducted tax, the assessee was not liable to make payment of short deducted tax.

In his return of income for the relevant assessment year 1997-98, the assessee claimed credit of the tax deducted at source by his employer. According to him, the tax had been deducted by the employer every time the payment of salary was made to him, but the employer had not furnished Form No. 16 or any other relevant evidence to prove that the tax had been deducted from his salary. The assessee filed copies of the pay slips for two months to show that income-tax was deducted from those payments and as per the assessee, it was a prima facie evidence to show that the former employer had been deducting income-tax from his salary. However, the Assessing Officer was not satisfied with the said evidence. He, thus, rejected the assessee's claim of credit of tax on ground that in the absence of a statutory certificate, credit of TDS could not be given.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee-company filed annual returns under section 206 for the financial year 1995-96 on 24-5-1996. A survey was carried out at the premises of the assessee-company, during which the ITO found that certain payments were made to the employees on which tax was not deducted at source though the same was required to be deducted in accordance with the provisions of section 192. As the employer had failed to deduct tax of Rs. 2,36,45,731 from its employees, it was held to be a 'deemed defaulter' under section 201(1) and interest of Rs. 51,72,501 was levied on it under section 201(1A). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO in respect of the amount of tax but with regard to charging of interest, he held that there was no basis for charging the same on monthly-defaults basis and the same could only be charged as the shortfall worked out under section 201(1). On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's appeal holding that in view of the fact that the proceedings initiated by the Assessing Officer for the assessment years 1992-93 and 1993-94in respect of the alleged short deduction of TDS were not pursued, the assessee was under the bona fide belief that the tax was not deductible at source from the disputed payment and, therefore, the departmental authorities had failed to prove the assessee's mala fides for the alleged non-deduction of tax.

On appeal under section 260A :

For the assessment year 1993-94, i.e., during the financial year 1992-93, the assessee had paid salaries to its employees and had deducted tax at source on the basis of estimated incomes of the respective employees. In the course of survey proceedings, it was observed that the assessee had allowed exemption of leave travel allowance (LTA) without verifying the actual incurrence of the expenditure as required by the provisions of section 10(5), read with rule 2B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, and had reimbursed drivers’ salary to some of the employees but the same had not been valued at cost while considering its perquisite value. According to the ITO, the assessee had committed default within the meaning of section 201. The assessee contended that it had acted upon the declaration from the employees with regard to the details of the travel and in respect of reimbursement of drivers’ salary, the assessee relied upon rule 3(c)( ii). The ITO, however, passed an order under section 201 directing the company to pay the tax which was short deducted. The Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the assessee’s appeal.

On second appeal, the assessee contended that even if there was a shortfall in deduction of tax, conditions necessary for the applicability of section 201(1) and 201(1A) did not apply and in view of section 191, tax could not be recovered from the employer-company and that under the section, in any case, where income-tax has not been deducted, it shall be payable by assessee-employee directly.

The assessee had sold a property to a purchaser for a consideration of certain amount who deducted TDS at the rate of 1 per cent of the sale consideration amount as per the provisions of section 194-IA as the consideration was in excess of Rs.50 lakhs and paid balance amount to the assessee. However, the vendee had not deposited the TDS deducted in Government's account and had not given the required Form 16B for deduction of tax at source to the assessee. The assessee filed return and claimed credit of said TDS amount. However same was disallowed by CPC for reason that TDS deducted was not deposited.

The Commissioner (Appeals)-NFAC also upheld order of CPC.

The assessee filed on instant appeal to the Tribunal and contended that once purchaser of property had deducted tax at source out of payments due/paid to the assessee, but had not deposited tax withheld by it, the assessee should not suffer and credit TDS should be allowed to it.

From the details of tax deducted and paid it was found that from the salary paid to employees in a month, the assessee-company deducted certain amount of tax whereas only a part of that amount was remitted to Government account. On being asked, the assessee-company stated that in case of certain employees tax was excess deducted and deposited in the earlier months and, therefore, that amount out of the total tax deducted from the employees in this month was refundable to employees in whose case tax was excess deducted in the earlier months and balance was remitted to Government account. According to the ITO, tax once deducted could not be refunded and it had to be remitted to Government account and in case there had been excess deduction in any case then the employee could claim refund only in his own assessment by filing a return. He accordingly, held the appellant to be an assessee in default. The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

■

The assessee-company was engaged in execution of Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contracts for solar power plants and other electrical works.

■

A survey under section 133A(2A) was conducted to verify compliance with tax deduction at source provisions. It was noticed that during the relevant financial year, the assessee had incurred interest expenditure on loans and professional/consultancy fees on which tax was deductible under sections 194A and 194J.

■

The assessee had recorded interest expenditure payable to M/s Shapoorji Pallonji & Co. Pvt. Ltd. (SPPL) and deducted tax at source at concessional rate pursuant to certificate under section 197 but failed to deposit the same into Government treasury. Proceedings under sections 201(1) and 201(1A) were initiated treating the assessee as an assessee in default.

■

The assessee contended that no interest was actually paid during the year due to financial incapacity, that TDS entry was recorded only on accrual basis as per accounting standards, and that SPPL had duly offered the interest income to tax in its return and paid taxes thereon, supported by Form 26A.

■

The Assessing Officer rejected the explanation and raised demand under sections 201(1) and 201(1A).

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that since the payee had offered the income to tax and no actual payment of interest had been made, the assessee could not be treated as assessee in default and deleted the demand.

■

On revenue's appeal:

'S' had wrongly debited the assessee's unit account with the cost of certain tickets issued by it and, simultaneously, credited commission accrued thereon and had deducted tax thereon. Later on, 'S' realized that it had wrongly debited the assessee's unit with the cost of tickets and, accordingly, reversed the amount debited by it in respect of the tickets and commission thereon. The assessee claimed credit of TDS on account of certificates issued by 'S'. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee's claim on the ground that commission income had not accrued to the assessee because 'S' had reversed the entries. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal:

Respondent No. 6 company appointed the assessee as managing director with effect from 1-4-1996. During the period April to December 1996, respondent No. 6 paid certain amount of salary to the assessee after deducting TDS. Thereafter, dispute arose between the parties and ultimately respondent No. 6 terminated the services of the assessee in March 1997. On 30-9-1997, the assessee filed return of income for the assessment year 1997-98, inter alia, claiming credit of TDS. The return was processed and the Assessing Officer issued intimation under section 143(1)(a) denying credit of the TDS amount. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer raised a demand of TDS along with interest under sections 234A, 234B and 234C. The assessee then wrote various letters to the revenue to recover the TDS amount collected by respondent No. 6 and to compel it to issue TDS certificate in favour of the assessee. Instead of recovering the amount from respondent No. 6, the authorities initiated penalty proceedings under section 221(1) against the assessee and attached the bank account of the assessee for recovery of the tax amount along with the interest.

On writ :

During the course of survey it was found by the revenue that there was a short deduction of tax on payment to employees as the assessee-employer had considered reimbursement of expenses/actual expenses paid to the employees on account of various allowances. The Assessing Officer treated those various allowances as taxable for the purpose of TDS. He then worked out the short deduction of tax and consequential levy of interest. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) did not accept the contention of the assessee about lack of jurisdiction with the ITO (TDS) on the ground that there was a failure on the part of the employer to deduct tax in accordance with the provisions of the Act. On merits, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed part of amount of expenses and directed the Assessing Officer to recalculate interest chargeable under section 201(1A).

On second appeal :

■

The assessee-company/accused had deducted certain TDS amount for the relevant assessment year, but failed to deposit the same in the Government Account within the prescribed period.

■

The Assessing Officer/complainant filed a complaint before Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (ACMM) under section 276B read with section 278B.

■

The ACMM after considering the entire evidence held that the assessee-company was guilty for not depositing TDS deducted in the Government account. The assessee was sentenced with a sentence of fine of Rs.25 lakhs.

■

On appeal, the Sessions Court held that no offence was made out since the TDS along with fine stood deposited. The assessee was accordingly acquitted.

■

The revenue filed a criminal appeal before the High Court under section 378 CrPC:

The assessee filed his return claiming credit of tax deducted at source by his employer.

However, without giving credit of the TDS deducted by his employer on the salary income as well as on the amount received towards professional and technical fees received from 'A' Limited, the department raised the demand by impugned notice issued under Section 221(1).

On writ:

The assessee filed its income tax return.

The Assessing Officer passed order under section 143(1) and disallowed deduction in respect of employees contribution towards PF & ESI received by assessee by invoking provisions of section 36(1)(va) read with section 43B on ground that same was not deposited with Government within time specified under the respective acts.

On appeal, the Commissioner upheld the decision of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal to the Tribunal :

■

The assessee was a local authority set up by the Government of Gujarat under section 22 of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976. During the year, the assessee had paid leave encashment to 11 retiree employees. The assessee had not deducted TDS on the leave encashment paid.

■

The Assessing Officer treated the assessee as in default under section 201(1) and 201(1A) on ground that the payments were in excess of Rs. 3 lakhs, and since the recipients were neither State Government nor Central Government employees, the exemption limit could not exceed Rs.3 lakhs and accordingly the tax had to be deducted by the disbursing authorities.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also confirmed the addition on the grounds that the employees of the assessee were neither State Government nor Central Government employees.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

The assessee-company deducted an amount as TDS but failed to credit the amount in the account of the Central Government. However, later on, the assessee credited the amount of the TDS with interest. A show-cause notice was issued against the assessee. In the reply the assessee submitted that it was not a case of no payment of TDS as said amount was already paid. Delay was made because there was shortage of funds with assessee. The assessee, therefore, contended that there was a 'reasonable cause' for the non-payment of amount within the prescribed period.

However, the Commissioner granted sanction to prosecute the assessee for offence committed under section 276B and section 278. He observed that the assessee had a wrong impression that it had compensated the Government by paying interest on delayed deposit of TDS and hence not prosecutable. Further, non-deposit of TDS in time due to shortage of funds was not a reasonable and justifiable because the deductor was just beholder of the tax payable by the deductee which should be deposited in time so that deductee might get the credit of such TDS. The deductor-assessee had taken plea of pending refunds with Income-tax Department. However, it was silent on the pending scrutiny assessments or appeals, etc. and then provisions of law under section 143(1D). Thus, refunds if any were lying with the department were under some authority of law. Moreover, refund was its own money and TDS belonged to the Government to be deposited on behalf of the deductees. Hence, it was not a justifiable ground. The assessee could not be granted immunity from prosecution merely on the ground that ultimately TDS was deposited in government account albeit lately.

On writ:

■

The assessee, a foreign company, was beneficial owner in American Depository Receipts (ADRs) of V Ltd which were held through a broker, CS. Later, V Ltd. announced the compulsory redemption of the ADR program and Citibank was appointed as the depository to manage the redemption process.

■

Upon redemption, the Citibank NA withheld tax at 43.68 per cent on the gross proceeds as the assessee did not have PAN and failed to provide necessary details before cut-off date.

■

Subsequently, the assessee obtained PAN and filed a revised return declaring income from the redemption of ADRs under section 115AC and claimed TDS credit.

■

The Assessing Officer denied the TDS credit on the grounds that the TDS was not reflected in Form 26AS.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer on ground that the assessee had not adequately complied with rule 37BA which mandates specific procedures for crediting TDS when income is assessable in the hands of a person other than the deductee and had failed to take sufficient actions to ensure the transfer of TDS credit.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee was a software company. During a survey conducted in its premises, it was noticed that massive amount of tax deducted at source from payment under the heads salaries, payment to contractors, professional fees for technical services, rent, etc., had been retained by the assessee without making remittance to the department.

The Assessing Officer levied the penalty under section 271C upon the assessee equal to the amount of tax recovered at source and withheld by the assessee without remittance to the department on due dates.

On appeal, both, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal, upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

The High Court dismissed the appeal preferred by the assessee by holding that failure to deduct/remit TDS would attract penalty under section 271C.

On the assessee's appeal to the Supreme Court -

■

The petitioner/assessee was a registered partnership firm and had filed its return of income for assessment year 2007-08 declaring a total income of ₹2.21 crores. The said return was processed under section 143(1) and an intimation was issued, whereby the TDS which was covered in the TDS certificate issued by company 'F' was rejected.

■

Thereafter, the assessee filed an application under section 154, for rectification of the error on record inasmuch as the credit for the TDS by company 'F' had not been accounted for. The assessee’s request was not processed. Consequently, the assessee sent a reminder requesting the Assessing Officer to pass an appropriate order. The assessee did not receive any response to the said reminder as well.

■

Thereafter, the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 221(1) for recovery of the demand, which had arisen solely for the reason that the TDS certificate furnished by the assessee had not been accounted for. The assessee responded to the said notice and requested the Assessing Officer to allow the credit for the TDS certificate.

■

The record indicates that the Assessing Officer sought verification of the deduction and deposit of TDS from the company 'F' – the entity that had deducted the TDS. Company 'F' responded to the Assessing Officer confirming that it had deducted TDS from payments made to the assessee and had also deposited the same to the credit of the Government.

■

Notwithstanding that all requisite details of the deposit of TDS had been furnished to the Assessing Officer, the Assessing Officer did not process the assessee’s request for according it the credit for the TDS. This was for the reason that the same was not verified from the data available on the portal.

■

Apparently, the Assessing Officer had sent a communication to the concerned Deputy Commissioner (TDS), Chandigarh enclosing therewith the copy of the TDS Certificates furnished by the assessee and requesting that the same be verified in order to enable the Assessing Officer to process the assessee's application. The concerned authority had responded stating that the data on the TRACES Portal was available from financial year 2007-08 and this data was not available for financial year 2006-07. Further, the ITR information was also not readily available for the said period.

■

On writ:

■

The assessee-company, a Multi-System Operator in the cable TV business, had deducted TDS but did not deposit it within the stipulated time, stating thatfunds were diverted to meet mandatory digitization requirements.

■

The company later deposited the entire deducted TDS to the credit of the Central Government and paid statutory interest under section 201(1A) for delayed payment.

■

However, a criminal complaint was filed alleging failure to deposit TDS within time.

■

The Special Judge, Economic Offences took cognizance for offences under section 276B read with section 278B against the company and its responsible officers.

■

On petition to the High Court :

The assessee filed its return declaring certain taxable income. The Assessing Officer, found that the TDS return for the assessment year in question along with proof of payment of TDS was not submitted. The assessee admitted that TDS had not been deducted in respect of the payments made/deemed to have been made who followed the mercantile system. It was also admitted that the TDS deducted had not been deposited to the credit of the Central Government.

The Assessing Officer as well as the Tribunal held that where assessee was liable to deduct and pay over TDS under section 194C and the assessee failed to do so, said payments were to be disallowed under section 40(a)(ia).

On appeal:

The assessee, a pilot by profession, was an employee of Kingfisher Airlines which had deduced the tax at source from his salary for the assessment years 2010-11 to 2012-13.

The Assessing Officer issued on the assessee notice seeking recovery of outstanding demand for the assessment years 2011-12 and 2012-13.

The assessee approached the employer requesting to furnish the certificate in relation to the tax deducted at source. The employer issued a certificate dated 19-11-2015 along with the computation of salary to the assessee stating that Form No. 16 was under process and filing of annual TDS return will be completed shortly. In the meantime the promoter of Kingfisher Airlines got bankrupt and on 11-3-2016 the Government of India - Ministry of Finance circulated office memorandum amongst all the Income-tax Departmental Officers directing them not to raise any demand of taxes on account of mismatch of credit of TDS due to non-payment of TDS by the Kingfisher Airlines.

On writ:

According to the Assessing Officer, the amounts deposited representing employees' contribution to provident fund and employees' state insurance beyond the statutory due date. The said sum was deducted from the salaries wages of the employees but were not credited to the respective funds within the statutory date and accordingly includible to the assessee's income in terms of section 2(24)(x) read with section 36(1)(va).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal, to the Tribunal:

The assessee provided services to a company known as Clutch Auto Ltd. (CAL), and made payment with the total value of the services amounting to Rs. 8,50,26,199. CAL, as the deductor, deducted tax at source from the payments made to the assessee, totalling Rs. 24,96,199. The assessee claimed that CAL did not fully deposit the deducted tax with the revenue department. Additionally, the assessee alleged that the balance amount, after tax deduction, was not remitted to them by CAL, and this issue was under consideration at the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). According to the assessee, CAL only deposited Rs. 69,897 as tax deducted at source, leaving a deficit of Rs. 24,26,302. This aspect was not disputed by the revenue department. The assessee's grievance was that they were not given credit for the tax deducted at source by CAL, which was not deposited with the revenue.

Consequently, a demand of Rs. 15,24,840 was raised against the assessee.

The assessee sought a writ of mandamus or other appropriate directives to compel the revenue department to refund the amount of Rs. 11,39,870 due to them for the assessment year 2011-12.

The High Court relied on the decision of in the case of Sanjay Sudan v. Asstt. CIT [2023] 148 taxmann.com 329/292 Taxman 138/452 ITR 107 (Delhi), and concluded that the revenue department could not indirectly recover tax that could not be directly collected from the deductee, as this would contravene section 205. Consequently, by an order dated 31-5-2023 the court ordered the revenue department to refund the sum of Rs. 11,39,870 to the assessee.

The revenue, filed review application and sought for review of order dated 31-5-2023 by contending that Form 16A was not produced as evidence of tax deduction.

On examination of the return filed by the assessee, the ITO found that the assessee had not deducted full tax due from two of the employees, K and J. The ITO held that the short deduction in each case had rendered the assessee liable to the provisions of section 201(1) and, therefore, issued demand notice. On appeal, the assessee contended before the AAC that amount in case of K was not deducted owing to the fact that an undertaking was furnished by him to the effect that he would deposit that amount at the time of filing his return, and that the disputed amount was deposited subsequently by the employee concerned. The assessee also contended that J was given a rebate on account of HRA, as declared by him. The AAC held that the statutory obligation cast upon the assessee had not been fulfilled and the explanation given by the assessee was not satisfactory. He, therefore, upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal :

A complaint was lodged by Assistant Commissioner Income-tax Department stating that the assessee-firm, accused No. 1 and its the principal officer, accused No. 2 deducted TDS amount for the financial year 2016-17 but failed to credit the same to the account of Central Government of India. Therefore, the accused No. 2 on behalf of the accused No. 1 committed offence punishable under section 276B.

The assessee filed instant petition with prayer to quash complaint. The assessee submitted that the TDS amount deducted by it was deposited with certain delay, however, in terms of section 201(1A), the amount was deposited along with interest. According to assessee once the TDS amount had been deposited along with the interest there was no occasion to initiate the prosecution under sections 276B and 278B.

During the financial year 1988-89 relevant to assessment year 1989-90, two companies namely L and P had paid interest due to the assessee after deducting tax at source. On 29-11-1989, the assessee filed loss return and claimed refund of tax paid by it which, inter alia, included the amount of tax deducted at source under section 194A by two companies viz. ‘L’ and ‘P’. ‘L’ and ‘P’ had failed to deposit the TDS amount deducted from the income of the assessee with the Department within the time prescribed and, therefore, the income-tax authorities initiated action against them. However, on writ petition, the High Court permitted them to deposit the TDS amount with the Department in instalment up to 15-4-1990 and both the companies had deposited the TDS amount in the Government treasury on or before 15-4-1990. The Assessing Officer, by intimation under section 143(1)(a) made prima facie adjustments such as additional tax under section 143(1A) to the loss return filed by the assessee and after giving credit of pre-paid tax which included sum being tax deducted at source by the aforesaid two companies and adjusting the TDS liability, determined the refund payable to the assessee and interest under section 244A. Subsequently, the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 154 calling upon the assessee to show cause as to why the intimation should not be rectified by withdrawing the credit of TDS given to the assessee as the TDS amounts were in fact not paid to the Central Government by the said companies on the date on which the return of income was filed by the assessee. The assessee contended that the said two companies had paid the TDS amount to the Department within the time allowed by the High Court and under section 205, the income-tax authorities could not demand the TDS amount from the assessee for the failure of the said companies, which deducted the tax, to pay to the Central Government and, accordingly, the credit for the TDS amount with interest granted under section 244A could not be withdrawn. Rejecting the contention of the assessee, the Assessing Officer passed the rectification order under section 154 thereby withdrawing the credit of TDS as well as the interest amount granted under section 244A and raised a demand. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer adjusted the said demand against refund payable to the assessee for next assessment year.

held.text:
■

The brief facts show that assessee is an employee of D. From the verification of the salary slips, it is apparent that tax is deducted from the salary of the employee by the employer. The employer has not deposited the tax to the credit of the Central Govt. Due to this, there was no credit appearing in Form 26AS of the assessee. Due to this, credit was denied by the Assessing Officer. [Para 7]

■

On appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), direction was given to the Assessing Officer to give credit to the assessee of the TDS to the assessee if it appears in Form 26AS. Naturally when no tax is deposited by the employer after deducting tax from the salary of the employee, it will not appear in Form 26AS of employee. If the employer after deducting the tax does not deposit the same to the credit of the Central Govt., that cannot be a cause for denying the credit to the employee who has suffered the TDS by employer and the employer did not pay the tax. In fact TDS is an onerous responsibility cast upon the payer on behalf of the Govt. of India. In this case, the employer had already admitted to CIRP proceedings by order of NCLT under section 9 of IBC, 2016 vide order dated 6-8-2025. Therefore there is a moratorium available to the employer. However, the provisions of the penalty and prosecution against the responsible officer are still applicable in this case. In spite of all this, nothing is done by revenue. Assessee-employee cannot be denied the credit of taxes, when by filing the conclusive evidence, tax is deducted by the employer. [Para 8]

■

Accordingly, the Assessing Officer is directed to grant credit of the above TDS to the assessee within 60 days from the date of receipt of this order. [Para 10]

■

It is observed that the Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Aditya Deepak Nasta v. ITO (IT Appeal Nos. 3293/M/2024, dated 20.09.2024) has also dealt with an identical issue/situation, wherein though the employer had deducted the TDS but not deposited in the Government account and therefore benefit of TDS was denied to the assessee. The Co-ordinate Bench while analyzing the relevant provisions of law and the identical issue as involved in the instant case, ultimately granted relief to the assessee, and held that: "From the provisions of section 201, where an employer does not deduct or, after deducting, fails to pay the tax, such person is deemed to be an assessee in default. Under section 205, where tax is deductible at source, the assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax himself to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income. In cumulative effect, sections 201 and 205 make the employer, who failed to remit tax deducted at source, the person in default, and the employee cannot be called upon to pay such tax again. In Yashpal Sahni v. ACIT (2007) 293 ITR 539 (Bom), it was held that failure to issue Form 16 or deposit TDS does not shift liability from the employer to the employee, and the Revenue cannot recover the amount once again from the assessee. In Kartik Vijaysinh Sonavane v. DCIT 440 ITR 11 (Guj), it was held that the Department is precluded from denying the benefit of tax deducted at source by the employer and credit shall be given to the assessee. On the aforesaid analyzations, the assessee cannot be treated as assessee in default as per section 199 and recovery can be effected from the employer but not from the assessee. Consequently, the Assessing Officer was directed to grant the credit of TDS and re-compute the income accordingly." [Para 6.1]

■

As the issue is covered in favour of the Assessee by the aforesaid decision, hence on the same footing/direction the Assessee is entitled to get the benefit of the TDS deducted by his employer but not deposited in Government account. Thus, the AO is directed to grant the credit of TDS and re-compute the income of the Assessee accordingly. It is clarified that the Department is always at liberty and empowered to take appropriate action against the employer for recovery of TDS deducted, but not against the employee, for recovery of TDS amount deducted but not deposited by the employer, as per the provisions of law, as applicable. [Para 7]

■

In the result, the appeal filed by the Assessee stands allowed. [Para 8]

■

The Income Tax Department can give credit of TDS only to the extent of receipt. This is clear from a reading of section 199. The Gauhati High Court in CIT v. Om Praksh Gattani [2001] 117 Taxman 549/242 ITR 638 (Gauhati) that while recovery to the extent of deduction may not be possible against the assessee from whose income such tax has been deducted, the assessee cannot also straight away claim credit of the tax so deducted but not paid over to the Central Government by the deductor. This also seems to be the view taken by the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court in Aslam Checkar v. ITO [Writ Petition (L) No. 2442 of 2024, dated 10-9-2024]. It is the admitted case of the petitioners that the amounts deducted as TDS have not been remitted by the employer to the Central Government/Income Tax Department. Therefore, the petitioners cannot be granted the relief of a direction to the Income Tax Department to grant credit to the extent of tax deducted from their salaries by the entity in which they were working. They are also not entitled to a writ directing the Income Tax Department to cancel the demands pending against them even though the amounts (TDS) have not been remitted to the Central Government/Income Tax Department. This is the only way in which sections 199 and 205 can be harmoniously interpreted. The section heading of section 205 uses the words ‘direct demand on assessee’ indicating that the provision only bars recovery from the assessee and does not mandate the grant of a credit. This may raise a legitimate question - is not the denial of credit a recovery. Denial of credit may ultimately result in a recovery, if the proceedings against the de`1ductor under section 201 do not end in recovery. However, this does not lead me to give any other meaning to section 205. Accordingly, disagreement is recorded with the view taken by the Delhi High Court in Sanjay Sudan v. Asstt.. CIT [2023] 148 taxmann.com 329/292 Taxman 138/ 452 ITR 107 (Delhi), to the extent it holds that on deduction credit is immediately available to an assessee from whose income such deduction has been made even if such amount has not been paid over to the Central Government/Income Tax Department by the deductor. The instructions contained in the Office Memorandum (F.No.275/29/2014-IT(B) dated 11-3-2015) only deal with the aspect of initiation of recovery proceedings against a person from whose income a tax deduction has been made and does not deal with the question as to whether credit of such unpaid amounts of TDS has to be given to such person. [Para 5]

■

Therefore, these writ petitions will stand disposed of holding that the petitioners are not entitled to the credit of any amount of TDS deducted from their salaries but not paid over to the Income Tax Department by the entity in which they were working. The petitioners are also not entitled to a writ directing the Income Tax Department to cancel the demands pending against them even though the amounts (TDS) have not been remitted to the Central Government/Income Tax Department. It will be open to the Income Tax Department to proceed against the entity for non-payment of TDS deducted from the salaries of the petitioners by treating the entity as an assessee in default under section 201. If any amount is paid by the entity or recovered from it, credit to the extent of such payment/recovery shall be given to the petitioners in these cases and demands to the extent of such recovery will be effaced. [Para 6]

From the language of section 205, it is clear that once the tax is deducted at source, the same cannot be levied once again on the assessee who has suffered the deduction. Once it is established that the tax has been deducted at source from the salary of the employee, the bar under section 205 comes into operation and it is immaterial as to whether the tax deducted at source has been paid to the Central Government or not, because elaborate provisions are made under the Act for recovery of tax deducted at source from the person who has deducted such tax. [Para 20]

In the instant case, the assessee had furnished monthly pay slips and bank statement to show that from his salary tax was deducted at source by the employer. Authenticity of the said pay slips and bank statements had not been disputed by the revenue. Thus, it was clear that the tax had been deducted at source by respondent No. 6 from the salary paid to the assessee. [Para 21]

In the instant case, though respondent No. 6 had deducted the tax at source from the salary income of the assessee, yet respondent No. 6 had not issued the TDS certificate in Form No. 16 to the assessee. As a result, the assessee was not entitled to avail credit of the tax deducted at source. However, once it is established that the tax has been deducted at source, the bar under section 205 comes into operation and the revenue is barred from recovering the TDS amount once again from the employee from whose income, TDS amount has been deducted. It is pertinent to note that the purpose of issuing TDS certificate under section 203 is to enable the assessee to avail credit of the tax deducted at source in the relevant assessment year. If the TDS certificate is not issued, then under section 199, the assessee from whose income tax has been deducted at source will not be entitled to take credit of the said amount. In that event, on account of the non-availability of the credit, the assessee would be liable to pay tax once again even though the tax was deducted at source. Thus, it would be a case of double taxation, which is not permissible in law. To avoid such anomaly, section 205 has been enacted, to the effect that, once the tax is deducted at source by the employer-company, then, the person from whose income, the tax has been deducted at source shall not be called to pay the said tax again. From the language of section 205, it is clear that the bar operates as soon as it is established that the tax has been deducted at source and it is wholly irrelevant as to whether the tax deducted at source is paid to the credit of the Central Government or not and whether TDS certificate in Form No. 16 has been issued or not. Also the mere fact that the employer may not issue TDS certificate to the employee does not mean that the liability of the employer ceases. The liability to pay income-tax if deducted at source is upon the employer. [Para 22]

Once the mode of collecting tax by deduction at source is adopted, that mode alone is to be adopted for recovery of tax deducted at source. Although it is obligatory on the part of the person collecting tax at source to pay the said TDS amount to the credit of the Central Government within the stipulated time, yet if such person fails to pay the TDS amount within the stipulated time, then section 201 provides that such person shall be deemed to be an assessee-in-default and the revenue will be entitled to recover the TDS amount with interest at 12 per cent per annum and till the said TDS amount with interest is recovered there shall be a charge on all the assets of such person or the company. Penalty under section 221 and rigorous imprisonment under section 276B, can also be imposed upon such defaulting person or the company. Thus, a complete machinery is provided under the Act for recovery of tax deducted at source from the person who has deducted such tax at source and the revenue is barred from recovering the TDS amount from the person from whose income, tax has been deducted at source. Therefore, the fact that the revenue is unable to recover the tax deducted at source from the person who has deducted such tax would not entitle the revenue to recover the said amount once again from the employee-assessee, in view of the specific bar contained in section 205. [Para 23]

tax deducted at source from the person who has deducted such tax at source and the revenue is barred from recovering the TDS amount from the person from whose income, tax has been deducted at source. Therefore, the fact that the revenue is unable to recover the tax deducted at source from the person who has deducted such tax would not entitle the revenue to recover the said amount once again from the employee-assessee, in view of the specific bar contained in section 205. [Para 23] In the instant case, the assessee had established that from his salary income-tax had been deducted at source by the employer-respondent No. 6 and, therefore, the revenue had to recover the said TDS amount with interest and penalty from respondent No. 6 alone and the revenue could not seek to recover the said amount from the assessee in view of the specific bar contained under section 205. The fact that the assessee was not entitled to the credit of the tax deducted at source for the non-issuance of the TDS certificate by respondent No. 6, could not be a ground to recover the amount of tax deducted at source from the assessee. In other words, even if the credit of the TDS amount was not available to the assessee for want of TDS certificate, the fact that the tax had been deducted at source from salary income of the assessee would be sufficient to hold that as per section 205, the revenue could not recover the TDS amount with interest from the assessee once again. [Para 24]

In the result, the petition succeeded. As respondent No. 6 had deducted the tax at source from the salary income of the assessee, the revenue could not have recovered the said amount with interest from the assessee in view of the bar contained in section 205. Accordingly, the revenue was directed to refund to the assessee the amount of interest at the rate of 6 per cent from the date of recovery till the date of payment. Though the credit of the tax deducted at source was not available to the assessee, since the said liability was not recoverable from the assessee, the revenue was directed to earmark the said TDS liability as ‘not recoverable’ from the assessee. [Para 25]

holding the field till today. [Para 11]

■

Section 205 read with CBDT circular, referred to above, being statutory one, has to be adhered to in letter and spirit and to give effect to such provision, CBDT circular was issued on 01-06-2015 and the office memorandum was issued on 11-03-2016. Therefore, for tax credit mismatch cannot be enforced coercively against the petitioner-assessee. [Para 12]

■ Where the employer, had deducted tax at source from the salary of its employee-assessee but had not deposited the amount to the Central Government’s account, the Assessing Officer would not deny the benefit of tax deducted at source by the employer to assessee and shall give credit of TDS amount to him. [Para 14]

■

The facts and law, as discussed above, are directly applicable to the present case and in view of the provisions contained in section 205, which provides that where tax is deductible at the source the assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax himself to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income and its applicability is not depending upon the credit for tax being given under section 199. Thereby, the department shall not deny the benefit of tax deducted at source by the employer during the relevant financial years to the assessee. The credit of the tax shall be given to the assessee and if in the interregnum, any recovery or adjustment is made by the department, the assessee shall be entitled to the refund, with the statutory interest, within eight weeks from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment. [Para 15]

■

In the result, therefore, the writ petition is allowed. But, however, in the facts and circumstances of the case, there shall be no order as to costs. [Para 16]

The employer issued monthly pay-slips to the assessee, deducting tax at source throughout the year, which totals up to Rs. 9.05 lakhs. Howbeit, a sum of Rs. 8.21 lakhs was deducted at source by EWL from the salary but not deposited. Since the non-deposit of the tax at source did not get reflected in Form No. 26AS, this led to the processing of return under section 143(1) not allowing credit for such amount. Here, it is pertinent to mention that though the assessee continued to remain in the employment of EWL for whole of the year but salary from October, 2018 was not paid. The assessee submitted that insolvency proceedings against the employer company are in progress and till date no salary for the period October, 2018 onwards has been paid. The moot question is about allowing or otherwise of credit for tax deducted at source from the salary income, which was not deposited by the employer due to its own precarious financial condition. Admittedly, the amount of tax deducted at source to the tune of Rs. 8.21 lakhs has not gone to the coffers of the revenue. At the same time, it is equally true that such amount of tax was deducted at source from salary of the assessee for full year, even though salary was paid only for six months despite the assessee serving EWL for full year. [Para 4]

Section 15 provides that any salary due from employer whether paid or not is chargeable to tax under the head `Salaries'. This indicates that salary income becomes chargeable to tax at the time of either receipt or becoming due, whichever is earlier. If salary becomes due earlier and is paid later on, there arises no problem because employee gets the salary which became due earlier and got chargeable at the due stage only. A peculiar situation has arisen in which though the salary became due and offered by the assessee in terms of mandate of section 15, but it was not paid for the last six months of the year under consideration. There is no corresponding provision in the Act bailing out an employee from getting deduction of such salary, which was included in the total income on due basis, but remained unpaid. [Para 5]

Be that as it may, the exact situation of concern is the Intimation issued by the Central Processing unit under section 143(1) in which the credit for Rs. 8.21 lakhs was not allowed because the amount was not deposited by the employer. In this regard, it would be relevant to take note of the prescription of section 143(1) dealing with the processing of return. Clause (a) of section 143(1) provides for making certain adjustments to the income declared for determining the total income. Clause (b) states that the taxes, interest and fee, if any, shall be computed on the basis of the total income computed under clause (a). Clause (c), which is material provides that the sum payable by, or the amount of refund due to, the assessee shall be determined after adjustment of the tax, interest and fee, if any, computed under clause (b) by any tax deducted at source, any tax collected at source, any advance tax paid, any relief allowable under section 89, any relief allowable under an agreement under section 90 or section 90A, or any relief allowable under section 91, any rebate allowable under Part A of Chapter VIII, any tax paid on self-assessment and any amount paid otherwise by way of tax, interest or fee. [Para 6]

The office memorandum dated 11-3-2016 shows the non-deposit of tax deducted at source by the deductor - recovery of demand against the deductee assessee. The Board issued the directions that in case an assessee whose tax has been deducted at source but is not deposited to the Government's account by the deductor, the assessee shall not be called upon to pay the demand to the extent tax has been deducted from his income. It was also specified that section 205 puts a bar on direct demand against the assessee in such cases and the demand on account of tax credit mismatch in such situations cannot be enforced effectively. As some of such directions of Board were not being strictly followed, the Board had reiterated the instruction contained in its letter dated 1-6-2015 directing the Assessing Officers not to enforce demands created on account of mismatch of credit due to non-payment of TDS amount to the credit of the Government by the deductor. [Para 9]

Here the assessee a pilot by profession was an employee of Kingfisher Airlines which had deducted the tax at source from his salary for the assessment years 2010-11 to 2012-13. It is not in dispute that such amount had not been deposited by the Airlines to the Central Government's account and, therefore, when the credit was claimed by the assessee, obviously, the same was not given. Hence the demand was raised with interest. [Para 10]

Section 205 is to the effect that assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax himself to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income. Its applicability is not dependent upon the credit for tax deducted being given under section 199. [Para 11]

The Assessing Officer shall not deny the benefit of tax deducted at source by the employer during the relevant assessment years to the assessee. The credit of the tax shall be given to the assessee and if in the interregnum any recovery or adjustment is made by the department, the assessee shall be entitled to the refund with the statutory interest. [Para 12]

■

The assessee was employed with employer and received salary which was paid to the assessee after deduction of tax at source. The assessee was also issued TDS Form showing full amount of Tax Deducted at source. However, the employer company did not deposit the same in the government treasury resulting into mismatch between the TDS as claimed by the assessee as per form 16/16A Vis-a-vis form 26AS as appearing in the portal of the Revenue. Once the tax is deducted by the employer, the assessee employee cannot be forced to make good short fall in deposit of tax by the employer. The revenue has to proceed against the employer for the recovery of said demand under section 200 and 201. However, in the present case the employer is already under liquidation. Therefore, the said action was also could not be taken against the employer. The non-deposit of TDS on the part of the employer cannot be slapped on the assessee more so no action against the employer can be taken under the Act. [Para 2.3]

■

Therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is set aside and the Assessing Officer is directed not to recover any demand from the assessee. The Assessing Officer can proceed against the employer to recover such demand or take any other remedial measure. Consequently, the appeal of the assessee is allowed. [Para 2.4]

■

A perusal of the instruction of the CBDT, as also the Office Memorandum, and the provisions of section 205 clearly shows that once a TDS has been deducted from the salary of an employee, it is deemed that taxes to such extent of the TDS deducted has already been paid by the said employee. The said employee cannot be revisited with the said taxes which has already been deducted. This being so, the Assessing Officer is directed to grant the assessee the benefit of the TDS which has been deducted from the salary of the employee. [Para 6]

■

In view of the provision of section 201, the revenue is very much at liberty to recover the TDS so deducted by the said employer. The failure on the part of the revenue to take appropriate action to recover the dues to it which has been collected on behalf of the revenue by a concerned cannot be treated as the failure on the part of the assessee to face a demand. This being so, the Assessing Officer is directed to grant the assessee to benefit of the credit of the TDS as claimed by the assessee. [Para 7]

■

In the result, the appeal of the assessee stands allowed. [Para 8]

The factual position pleaded by the assessee and admitted by the revenue is that the revenue raised multiple demands of outstanding income tax and interest pertaining to the relevant assessment years. It is also not in dispute that, as reflected from records, the assessee was being paid salary after deduction of tax at source but his employer did not deposit the same with the department. Despite repeated communications from assessee, the said demands were not withdrawn by the revenue. [Para 3]

The core issue to be considered by the Bench is as to whether any recovery towards the said outstanding tax demand can be effected against the assessee in view of the admitted position that the tax payable on salary of the assessee was being regularly deducted at source by his employer, who did not deposit the deducted tax with the department. [Para 4]

The Delhi High Court while deciding a similar issue in the case of Sanjay Sudan v. Asstt. CIT [2023] 148 taxmann.com 329/292 Taxman 138/452 ITR 107 observed that the assessee therein is right inasmuch as neither can the demand qua the tax withheld by the deductor/employer be recovered from him, nor can the same amount be adjusted against the future refund, if any, payable to him. [Para 5]

It is contended by the revenue that no credit for tax can be given to the assessee, since in view of the provisions under section 199 the credit can be given only when the tax which was deducted at source is paid to the Central Government and in the instant case admittedly the tax deducted from salary of the assessee has not been deposited by his employer. This contention was raised also in the case of Sanjay Sudan (supra) but not accepted by the court. [Para 6]

The assessee having accepted the salary after deduction of tax at source had no further control over it in the sense that thereafter it was the duty of his employer acting as tax collecting agent of the revenue under Chapter XVII of the Act to pay the deducted tax amount to the department in accordance with law. The employer of the assessee having failed to perform his duty to deposit the deducted tax with the revenue, the assessee cannot be penalized. It would always be open for revenue to proceed against employer of the assessee for recovery of the deducted tax. [Para 8]

Section 199 cannot operate as impediment to grant relief to the assessee. [Para 9]

In view of the aforesaid, the demand of tax and interest raised against the assessee is set aside. The Assessing Officer is restrained from carrying out any recovery proceedings against the assessee. The Assessing Officer is further directed to refund the amount which was adjusted by him against the impugned demand. [Para 10]

The case is no longer res integra and is covered by the decision of this very Court rendered in case of Devarsh Pravinbhai Patel v. Asstt. CIT [R/SCA No. 12965 of 2018, dated 24-9-2018] where too, the petitioner was an employee of the Kingfisher Airlines and worked as a pilot. In his case also the TDS on the salary made to the petitioner had not been deposited. It is only when the department raised the tax demand with interest and initiated the actions of the recovery that this Court was approached. Relying on the decision of the Gauhati High Court rendered in case of Asstt. CIT v. Om Prakash Gattani [2001] 117 Taxman 549/[2000] 242 ITR 638, this Court allowed the same by holding that the petitioner-assessee deductee is entitled to credit of the tax deducted at source with respect to amount of TDS for which Form No. 16A issued by the employer deductor has been produced and consequently department is directed to give credit of tax deducted at source to the petitioner-assessee - deductee to the extent Form No. 16 A issued by the deductor have been issued. Consequently, the impugned demand notice is quashed and set aside. However, it is clarified and observed that if the department is of the opinion deductor has not deposited the said amount of tax deducted at source, it will always been open for the department to recover the same from the deductor. Thus, it is held that the Department cannot deny the benefit of tax deducted at source by the employer of the petitioner during the relevant financial years. Credit of such tax would be given to the petitioner for the respective years. If there has been any recovery or adjustment out of the refunds of the later years, the same shall be returned to the petitioner with statutory interest. [Para 7]

In case of Om Prakash Gattani (supra) Gauhati High Court was dealing with the TDS not deposited of prize money payable to the petitioner. It held and observed that a perusal of section 205 clarifies the position where it provides that where tax is deductible at source, the assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax himself to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income. What is noticeable in this provision is that its applicability is not dependent upon the credit for tax deducted being given under section 199. What is necessary for applicability of this provision is that the amount has been deducted from the income. In case where the amount has been deducted but not paid to the Central Government that eventuality is taken care of by section 201.The appellant could not show that under the law it maybe permissible to proceed against the assessee even after deduction of the tax at source, nor could it be held that merely by deduction of tax at source, credit for deduction of tax at source has to be given even though the amount may not have been made over to the Government treasury. As the mere deduction of tax at source would not close the chapter of tax liability unless it is deposited in the Government treasury. [Para 8]

The facts being almost identical, no separate reasoning are desirable and the petition is being allowed. The department is precluded from denying the benefit of the tax deducted at source by the employer during the relevant financial years to the petitioner. [Para 9]

The credit of the tax shall be given to the petitioner and if in the interregnum any recovery or adjustment is made by the respondent, the petitioner shall be entitled to the refund of the same, with the statutory interest, from the date of receipt of copy of this order. [Para 11]

Petition is accordingly disposed of. [Para 12]

For credit of tax deducted at source, various provisions have been prescribed in Act and Rules. The section 199 has prescribed certain procedure. As per sub-section (1) of section 199, if any deduction is made under the Chapter-XVII and paid to the Central Government, then same is to be considered as payment of tax on behalf of the person from whose income the deduction was made. The sub-section (3) authorize the CBDT to frame Rules for facilitating credit to be given in respect of tax deducted. The CBDT in terms of section 199(3) has framed rule 37BA. As per clause 4 of the rule 37BA, the credit of the tax deducted and paid to the Central Government shall be allowed on the basis of the information relating to deduction of tax furnished by the deductor to the Income-tax Authority or the person authorized by such authority and the information in the return of income in respect of the claim for the credit, subject to verification in accordance with the risk management strategy formulated by the CBDT from time-to-time. [Para 8.4]

As per section 203, every person deducting the tax shall issue a certificate to the effect that tax has been deducted specifying amount of tax so deducted, rate at which tax has been deducted. Under rule 31 framed under section 203, said TDS certificate should be issued in Form 16 in case deduction under section 192 annually or in Form 16A in case deduction of tax under any other section quarterly. [Para 8.5]

As per section 203AA, prescribed Income-tax Authority shall deliver to every person from whose income, tax has been deducted a statement in the prescribed form specifying amount of tax deducted or paid within prescribed time limit. As per rule 31AB framed thereunder, the Director General of Income-tax (Systems) shall deliver to every person whose tax has been deducted a statement referred to in section 203AA in the Form 26AS by the 31st July following the financial year during which taxes were deducted or paid. [Para 8.6]

Thus, from above it is evident that each deductor will issue Form 16/16A to every payee individually whereas the Income-tax Department will deliver the consolidated statement of tax deducted by various payees online in the Form 26AS. [Para 8.7]

Prior to introduction of Form 26AS, the credit of TDS was used to be given on the basis of TDS certificate produced by the assessee. The assessee has referred to the decision of the Bombay High Court in the case of Yashpal Sahni v. Rekha Hajarnavis, Asstt. CIT [2007] 293 ITR 539. In said case, a question was raised as to where a company deducts tax at source (TDS) from the salary payable to an employee, but fails to deposit the said amount into the Government treasury, whether, the revenue can recover the TDS amount with interest from the concerned employee inspite of the express bar contained in section 205 ? [Para 8.8]

The High Court after considering provisions of the law and precedents on the issue in dispute held that assessee should be provided credit of tax irrespective whether the tax deducted was deposited by the deductor into the Government account. [Para 8.9]

Thus in the above case, the High Court directed the Assessing Officer to allow credit of the TDS which was deducted by the payer of the income, irrespective whether the same was deposited in Government account or not. In the above case, the assessee was able to substantiate by way of the salary slips and his bank statement that tax was deducted by the payer of salary income despite that no TDS certificate was issued by the deductor to the assessee. [Para 8.10]

In the instant case, the assessee has submitted that no certificate of tax deduction at source are available with the assessee. Therefore, respectfully following the decision of the Bombay High Court in the case of Yashpal Shani (supra), for availing credit of TDS, the assessee has to discharge its responsibility of substantiating whether tax was deducted by the payer of income. From the contract agreement also it is evident that the borrower was required to intimate to the 'DZ Bank AG' regarding the amount of tax deducted at source and paid to the tax authority. The assessee has even neither furnished any details of the amount of TDS in respect of interest income, which it has shown if any in its profit and loss account, nor furnished any evidence to support deduction of tax at source by the payer of income. The assessee has not furnished any certified copies of ledger account of assessee in the books of borrower parties so as to reflect the amount credited in the account of the assessee. [Para 9]

Tax had been deducted from the salary of the assessee by the employer. In this view of the factual position, section 205 really put a bar against direct demand on the assessee. The interest leviable in respect of TDS also is a consequence of non-furnishing of certificate by the assessee in respect of TDS. Had the employer given the assessee a TDS certificate, no interest could be levied on the assessee as the same was to be reduced while computing assessed tax. However, at the same time, credit for tax deducted at source cannot be given to an assessee unless the assessee submits certificate as prescribed under section 203 in respect of TDS as per provisions of section 199. [Para 5]

Hence, in view of section 205, the authorities under no circumstances could make the assessee liable to make payment of any tax to the extent to which the tax had been deducted at source by the person paying the salary to the assessee under section 192. However, as TDS certificate had not been given by deductor, the credit of TDS could not be given. Under the peculiar circumstances of the case, the income-tax authorities were directed not to recover any tax levied on the assessee in respect of non-furnishing of TDS certificate. There are various provisions in the Act which provide the powers to the income-tax authorities to enforce the payment of tax by deductor and also enforce issue of certificate in respect thereof to the payee. There was no material on record to show that whether such powers had been exercised by the department to enforce the payment of tax deducted at source and also for the issue of certificate thereof. In that view of the situation, the assessee could not be held liable for the consequences which were beyond the control of the assessee, i.e., non-furnishing of TDS certificate. Till such powers were not exercised by the revenue authorities to corner the deductor of tax, i.e., to collect payment of TDS from him and also to obtain the certificate, no tax as well as interest pertaining thereto could be recovered from the assessee. The appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed in the aforesaid terms. [Para 6]

In the recent judgment delivered on 18-7-2007, in the case of Yashpal Sahni v. Asstt. CIT, the Bombay High Court held that once the employer has deducted the tax at source, the employee-assessee cannot be held responsible for the payment once again and any such demand raised against such employee-assessee, cannot be recovered. [Para 8]

In the instant case, the assessee had furnished the pay slips only for two months and there were no documentary evidences in respect of the remaining ten months. As the assessee was not in a position to procure the said details and certificate from his former employer, it was not possible to expect that the assessee would be able to file such details and evidences before the assessing authority.
