8.4-5 Credit for the tax deducted or collected - The provision in relation to :—

◆ TDS [section 199(3)], reads as follows: “where any deduction is made. . . on or after the 1st day of April, 2005 and paid to the Central Government, the amount of tax deducted and specified in the statement referred to in section 203AA shall be treated as tax paid on behalf of the person referred to in sub-section (1) . . . and credit shall be given to him for the amount so deducted in the assessment... without production of certificate.” (Emphasis supplied)

◆ TCS [first proviso to section 206C(4)] reads: “provided that where any amount is collected... on or after 1st day of April, 2005 and paid... to the credit of the Central Government, the amount of tax collected and specified in statement referred to... shall be deemed as payment of tax on behalf of the person from whom the amount has been collected and credit shall be given to him for the amount so collected in the assessment... without production of certificate.” (Emphasis supplied)

Thus, the amount of tax deducted/collected and specified in the Statement would be treated as tax paid on behalf of the payee/buyer. It appears, the payee/buyer would get credit for such tax deducted/collected on his/her behalf. For whatever reasons, the amount of tax deducted/collected is not specified in the Statement, the amount not specified would not be treated as tax deducted/collected on behalf of the payee/buyer and credit will not be available for the same to the payee/buyer.

In this connection an issue may arise about the treatment of tax deducted or collected and specified in the statement but not paid by the payer/collector. If appears that to the extent tax deducted/collected, whether specified in the statement or not the recovery cannot be enforced against the payee/buyer, for the following reasons :

(i) Section 203AA and second proviso to section 206C(5), respectively provide that the prescribed income-tax authorities or authorised person shall prepare and collect the statement of tax deducted/paid [under section 192(1A)] on tax collected.

(ii) Section 199(3) and first proviso to section 206C(4) treat the tax deducted or collected and specified in the statement as tax paid on behalf of the payee or buyer. Thus, the tax deducted on collected, whether paid or not is the relevant amount which can be considered as paid on behalf of the payee/buyer.

(iii) Section 205 of the Act provides that where the tax is deductible at source under applicable provisions of Chapter XVII, the assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income.

(iv) Section 191 contemplates direct payment by the payee only in a case where tax is deducted in terms of Chapter XVII and not in a case where the tax is deducted and not paid.

While claiming the credit, the payee or the buyer may face some difficulties on account of one or more of the following illustrative situations :

◆ The Statement is not received from the prescribed income-tax authority or authorised agency in time. In that case, his return of income would be delayed, with attendant consequences. Alternatively, he may not be able to claim credit for the same.

a case where the amount has been deducted by the person responsible to deduct the amount under the statutory provisions, the assessee has no control over the matter. In case of default in making over the amount to the account of the Central Government, it is obviously the person responsible to deduct or the person who has made the deduction who is held responsible for the same. The responsibility of such person is to the extent that he has to be deemed to be an assessee-in-default in respect of the tax. The amount of tax can be recovered by the department treating the person responsible to deduct tax at source as an assessee-in-default in respect of the tax. It will not be possible to proceed to recover the amount of tax from the assessee. The assessee cannot be doubly saddled with the tax liability. Deduction of tax at source is only one of the modes of recovery of tax. Once this mode is adopted and by virtue of the statutory provisions the person responsible to deduct the tax at source deducted the amount, only that mode should be pursued for the purpose of recovery of tax liability and the assessee should not be subjected to other modes of recovery of tax by recovering the amount once again to satisfy the tax liability.

In the light of the matter, the notices issued under section 226(3) to the bankers of the assessee to satisfy the tax liability from his bank account were illegal. It was not that the Income-tax Department was helpless in the matter. The person responsible to deduct the tax at source would move into the shoes of the assessee and he would be deemed to be an assessee- in-default. Whatever process or coercive measures were permissible under the law would only be taken against such person and not the assessee.

However, this would not mean that mere deduction of the tax amount at source would amount to total discharge of the tax liability so long as the amount deducted is not deposited in the coffers of the Central Government. According to section 199, credit for tax deducted is to be given when the amount is deducted and paid to the Central Government and a certificate of deduction is produced as furnished under section 203. There was no force in the assessee's submission that on mere deduction of the amount at source, credit for tax must be given and it could not be withheld even though the person responsible to deduct the tax at source had not made it over to the Central Government. Once credit on account of payment of tax is given, the tax liability will stand discharged. Any step to recover the amount of tax can be taken only in case the tax liability is not discharged and it still subsists. The note appended by the Assessing Officer in the order of assessment made it clear that credit for the amount deducted was not being given and that would be given only when evidence as to actual payment of the amount to the Central Government was furnished. But this position would not legally justify initiation of recovery proceedings against the assessee from whose income-tax had been deducted at source. The statutory scheme evolved to employ this mode of recovery of tax at source also points to the same position and rightly so. Section 201 aptly provides that the person responsible to deduct the tax would be deemed to be an assessee-in-default so that he can be proceeded against for recovery of the amount instead of the assessee who has already parted with the amount but due to some commission or omission on the part of the person responsible to deduct the amount at source over whose activity he has no control, he cannot be subjected to double payment of tax and brunt of arduous recovery proceedings. The provisions as contained in section 201 provide a kind of protection to the assessee where tax liability as standing against him is yet discharged and credit for the amount deducted cannot be given in terms of section 199.

Section 205 clarifies the position. Its applicability is not dependent upon the credit for tax deducted being given under section 199. What is necessary for applicability of this provision is that the amount has been deducted from the income. In case where the amount is deducted but not paid to the Central Govt., that eventuality is taken care of by section 201. Neither the revenue could show that under the law it might be permissible to proceed against the assessee even after deduction of the tax at source nor could it be held that merely by deduction of tax at source, credit for TDS had to be given even though the amount might not have been made over to the Government treasury. Therefore, while the note made by the Assessing Officer in the assessment order not giving credit on account of deduction of tax was to be upheld and the Single Judge's order was to be set aside to that extent, his order was to be maintained insofar as the quashing of the notices issued under section 226(3) was concerned.

Dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates [Sections 203 & 206C]

8.6 An assessee is entitled to credit in respect of tax deducted at source (‘TDS’) and tax collected at source (‘TCS’) on the basis of a certificate issued by the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source. Such certificate has to be enclosed with the return of income to claim the credit.

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 proposed dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates and, inter alia1, provided that on and after 1-4-2005:

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source should file quarterly statements with the income-tax authority or authorised person;

◆ such authority or person would furnish a statement of tax deducted or collected at source (‘the Statement’) to the payee or buyer;

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source need not furnish certificate to the payee or buyer; and

◆ the payee or buyer would be entitled to the credit for TDS or TCS based on the statement furnished by such authority or person.

The Finance Act, 2005 postponed the implementation of the above by a year and the Finance Act, 2006 further postponed it up to 31-3-2008.

Pending stabilisation of the system, the Finance Act, 2008 has amended with effect from 1-4-2008, the following provisions to provide that the amendments made therein by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004, as further amended by the Finance Act, 2005 and Finance Act, 2006 would become effective from 1-4-2010 instead of 1-4-2008 as provided heretobefore:

◆ Section 203(3) of the Act providing that a payer need not issue a certificate of TDS;

◆ First proviso to section 206C(5) providing that a person responsible for collecting tax at source need not issue a certificate of TCS.

Further, the Explanation below section 139(9) providing that if the proof of tax deducted or collected at source is not attached on or after 1-4-2008, the return would not be considered as defective has been amended by deleting the words ‘on or after 1st April, 2008’.

8.6-1 Analysis of amendments - The effect of the above amendments is as follows:

◆ the credit for TDS or TCS, in respect of the financial years 2008-09 and 2009-10 (assessment years 2009-10 and 2010-11) will be available on the basis of certificates issued by the payer or the person responsible for collecting tax at source; and

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source will have to continue to issue certificates to the payee or the buyer, in respect of the tax deducted or collected at source during the financial years 2008-09 and 2009-10.

Section 203AA of the Act provides that the prescribed authority shall furnish the statement of TDS in the prescribed form and specifying prescribed particulars. Similarly, the second proviso of section 206C(5) provides that the prescribed authority shall furnish such statement of TCS. The Finance Act, 2006 had postponed the applicability of these provisions to the financial year beginning on or after 1-4-2008. In Instruction No. 275/29/2014-IT(B) dated 1-6-2015 the Board recorded that taxpayers were being denied credit because deductors failed to deposit the tax, and directed that in such cases coercive recovery should not be enforced from the deductee. The subsequent Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016 reiterated the same position and directed field officers not to enforce demands created on account of mismatch of credit due to non-payment by the deductor. These directions are binding on the Department and are intended precisely to avoid double taxation of an innocent deductee. [Para 20]

It is important to remember that the assessee has already brought the corresponding income to tax. Denial of credit in the assessee’s hands, because the deductor failed to deposit or misreported the deduction, results in taxing the same income twice. Section 205 is the Parliamentary safeguard against precisely such injustice. The Board’s Instruction and Memorandum translate that safeguard into administrative practice. The High Courts have given it judicial benediction. The revenue’s proper remedy lies against the defaulting deductor under sections 200 and 201 and other enabling provisions, and not against the deductee who has already suffered deduction. [Para 24]

■

The revenue suggested that section 199 contemplates credit only on payment to the Government and hence the absence of 26AS entries should defeat the claim. Section 199 cannot be read in isolation. It must be read harmoniously with section 205. Section 199 allocates the time and manner of giving credit in the ordinary course when the deductor has discharged his obligation. Section 205 steps in to prevent a second exaction from the deductee when that ordinary course is derailed by the deductor’s default. The harmonious reading preserves both provisions and avoids the manifest unfairness that would otherwise ensue. [Para 25]

■

The view that the assessee must first secure rectification of the deductors’ e-TDS statements and only thereafter obtain credit cannot be subscribed to. The statute does not impose such a pre-condition. The deductee has neither control over nor access to the deductor’s filings. The insistence effectively makes the assessee hostage to another’s compliance and empties section 205 of content. The more correct and lawful approach is to verify the assessee’s primary evidence of deduction and allow credit accordingly, leaving the Department free to pursue the defaulting deductors in accordance with law. [Para 26]

■

In the result the assessee is entitled to credit of TDS to the extent deduction from its receipts is established on the basis of the contemporaneous material placed on record. The denial of credit by Assessing Officer and its affirmation by the first appellate authority are set aside. The Assessing Officer is directed to verify the assessee’s reconciliation with reference to the invoices, payment advices and bank statements already on record and to allow the corresponding credit of TDS. This direction is squarely in line with section 205, CBDT Instruction dated 1-6-2015 and Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016, and the principles laid down by the Bombay and Delhi High Courts noticed above. [Para 27]

■

Once credit is so allowed the levy of interest under sections 234B and 234C does not survive. Even otherwise, when the tax liability stands met through deduction at source and the difference is occasioned solely by the deductor’s lapse, fastening compensatory interest upon the deductee would be unjust and contrary to the scheme of the Act. The Assessing Officer shall therefore delete the interest charged under sections 234B and 234C while giving effect to this order. [Para 28]

■

For the reasons aforesaid the appeal is allowed. The Assessing Officer shall give effect to this order by granting due credit of TDS on verification of the material on record and by deleting the consequential interest, in accordance with law. [Para 29]

On appeal to the Tribunal:

It was quite evident from the TDS certificate dated 29-3-2004 issued by the deductors that the tax was actually deducted and paid into Government treasury only on 29-3-2004. From the record, it was found that the assessee had disclosed interest income receivable from two companies. However, during the years under consideration, the assessee neither actually received any interest, nor any certificate was given for deduction of tax at source. It appeared that there was some dispute between the assessee and its associates concerns to whom loans were given on interest. When the dispute was resolved, the tax was deducted at source for the period 1-4-2002 to 31-3-2003 on the amount credited to the assessee’s account; the tax so deducted was also deposited in the Government treasury on 29-3-2004 and a certificate dated 29-3-2004 was also issued to the assessee. As per the provisions of section 199, the credit for TDS has to be given in the assessment year in which the income relating to the tax deducted is assessed to tax. It also stipulates for giving credit to the assessee only on the production of certificate furnished under section 203. In the instant case, the TDS certificate furnished by the assessee clearly indicated that it pertained to the period 1-4-2002 to 31-3-2003 in respect of amount paid/credited, on which the deductors had deducted tax at source on 29-3-2004. Under the provisions of sections 194B, 199, 201, 203 and 205, a person responsible for making the payment to the assessee is under a statutory obligation to deduct tax at source and after deduction of the amount of tax, he is required to deposit the same to the credit of the Central Government and to issue a certificate of deduction. The assessee is entitled to claim credit for amount deducted at source only when the amount so deducted is found to be actually deposited to the credit of the Central Government and a certificate under section 203 is also furnished to this effect. Only on payment of amount to the credit of the Central Government, it would be treated as payment of tax. Accordingly, a mere claim of deduction of tax at source, or mere disclosing the respective income receivable in its books of account without any corresponding deduction of tax at source, would not entitle the assessee to claim credit of tax relatable to such income. So long as the amount deducted is not deposited in the coffers of the Central Government, there is no question of giving any credit for such amount of tax. But once tax is deducted on the income credited by the assessee in its books of account and a requisite certificate to this effect is issued by deductor after deposit of tax amount in the Government treasury, the assessee becomes entitled to the credit of such TDS, while computing the tax liability for the relevant period. [Para 5]

The scheme for giving credit for TDS has been modified through clauses 56 and 59 of the Finance Bill, 2002. [Para 6]

Consequence of failure to deduct or pay [Section 201]

8.5 Under section 201, a person is deemed to be an assessee-in-default if there is a failure to deduct tax at source or for failure to deposit the tax deducted at source after such tax has been deducted. The persons covered under the ambit of section 201 are:

(i) person referred to in section 200;

(ii) the principal officer and the company of which he is the principal officer in the cases referred to in section 194 [relating to deduction of tax at source on dividends].

Section 200(1) provides that any person deducting any tax at source in accordance with the provisions of Chapter XVII shall pay the sum so deducted to the Central Government or as the Board directs within the prescribed time. Since section 200 applies to persons deducting tax, and since it has been used in section 201, a view has been expressed that the provisions of section 201(1) do not cover failure to deduct tax at source. In order to counter this view, section 201(1) has been substituted with effect from 1-6-2002 to clarify that where a person, including the principal officer of a company,

(i) who is required to deduct any sum in accordance with the provisions of the Act; or

(ii) referred to in section 192(1A), being an employer,

does not deduct, or after so deducting fails to pay, or does not pay, the whole or any part of the tax, as required by or under the Act, he shall be deemed to an assessee in default under section 201.

A similar amendment has also been carried out in Explanation to section 191 with retrospective effect from 1-6-2003.

Dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates [Sections 203 & 206C]

8.6 An assessee is entitled to credit in respect of tax deducted at source (‘TDS’) and tax collected at source (‘TCS’) on the basis of a certificate issued by the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source. Such certificate has to be enclosed with the return of income to claim the credit.

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 proposed dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates and, inter alia1, provided that on and after 1-4-2005:

◆ such authority or person would furnish a statement of tax deducted or collected at source (‘the Statement’) to the payee or buyer;

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source need not furnish certificate to the payee or buyer; and

◆ the payee or buyer would be entitled to the credit for TDS or TCS based on the statement furnished by such authority or person.

Pending stabilisation of the system, the Finance Act, 2008 has amended with effect from 1-4-2008, the following provisions to provide that the amendments made therein by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004, as further amended by the Finance Act, 2005 and Finance Act, 2006 would become effective from 1-4-2010 instead of 1-4-2008 as provided heretobefore:

◆ Section 203(3) of the Act providing that a payer need not issue a certificate of TDS;

Further, the Explanation below section 139(9) providing that if the proof of tax deducted or collected at source is not attached on or after 1-4-2008, the return would not be considered as defective has been amended by deleting the words ‘on or after 1st April, 2008’.

The assessees were salaried employees of ASPL. Tax at source (TDS) was deducted from their salaries but was not remitted by the employer to the Income Tax Department.

■

Due to such non-remittance, the assessee’s faced tax demands.

■

In the instant writ, the assessees contended that they should not be liable for TDS not deposited by the employer.

This was not a case where no tax at all had been deducted in complete breach and violation of law. Thus, at the most, it could be a case of short deduction of tax. On the other hand, section 201 does not envisage a situation of short deduction of tax in order to deem an assessee to be in default. Section 192 is very categorical to state that tax has to be deducted from the head ‘Salaries’ computed on the estimated income of the assessee under this head for the concerned financial year. What has to be seen is whether the employer-company has acted bona fide or not while computing the tax liability of its employees for the purposes of deducting tax at source. Considering the facts of the instant case, it could not be gainsaid that the assessee-company did act fairly and in a bona fide manner. As held in State Bank of Patiala v. CIT [1999] 236 ITR 281 (Punj. & Har.), it is not open for the employer-company to suspect that several assessee-employees had filed bogus declaration. The same view could be taken with regard to the action of the assessee-company in relying upon section 3(c)( ii) for adopting the amount with regard to the taxability of reimbursement of drivers’ salary. Thus, on the facts of the case, it had to be held that in the case, the company had honestly and fairly formed an opinion and arrived at the estimated income of the employees for the purposes of section 192.

The second argument of the assessee that section 201 does not apply to short deduction of tax, had also to be accepted. Both, sub-section (1) as well as sub-section (1A) of section 201 speak only of two situations, viz., (a) where the company has failed to deduct tax at all; and (b) where having deducted the tax, the company has failed to pay the tax to the credit of the Central Government. In the instant case, neither situation existed. It was a case where company had deducted tax and paid it to the Central Government. At the most it was a case of short deduction of tax, for which section 201 cannot be applied.

As per section 191 there is a mandate on the taxing authority to recover tax which is not deducted, only from the assessee and not from the payer of the income. The legal proposition that charging provision has to be strictly construed is an established position of law. Chapter XVII is titled as ‘Collection and recovery of tax’. As the title itself suggests the Chapter contains machinery provisions and does not deal with substantive law of creating a charge. It is section 4(1) which creates substantial charge on the person who earns the income. Primarily, it is his duty to pay tax on that income. The provisions of Chapter XVII are merely to accelerate the process of collection and recovery of tax and, therefore, these provisions cast an obligation on the payers of certain incomes to deduct tax at source. However, this does not denude the primary charge put on the recipient of the income. The primary charge on the recipient of the income is, therefore, not transferred to the payer of the income. It is with a view to clarify the basic legal position that section 191 is enacted and placed just before the machinery for deducting tax at source starts rolling. This is also confirmed by sub-section (2) of section 190 which makes it clear that the collection and recovery of tax will not prejudice the charge created by section 4(1). Thus, at the cost of repetition it has to be emphatically stated that there is nothing in section 191 whereby the primary obligation of the assessee is transferred to the payer of the income in the event of failure to deduct tax thereon under Chapter XVII.

8.4-4 The Statement - Note the following :

♦

The prescribed income-tax authority or the authorised agency has to prepare the Statement. The Statement would be prepared on the basis of the quarterly statements filed by the payer or the collector. However, there is no specific reference to the same in the provision.

♦

The completeness/accuracy of the Statement would depend on the timeliness and quality of the quarterly statements.

♦ The prescribed income-tax authority or the authorised agency has to deliver the Statement to the payee/buyer. There is no requirement about furnishing a copy of the Statement to the Assessing Officer of the payee/buyer.

♦

The Statement, in respect of TDS, should specify the amount of tax deducted or paid [under section 192(1A)] and other particulars as may be prescribed. Thus, the Statement would contain details of the tax deducted as per the provisions of the Chapter and paid under section 192(1A).

♦

The Statement, in respect of TCS, should specify the amount of tax collected.

♦

Thus, it may be noted that the Statement must specify:

■

TDS Statement:

•

Amount of tax deducted as per the provisions of the Chapter; and/or

•

Amount of tax paid under section 192(1A); and/or

•

Such other particulars as may be prescribed.

■

TCS Statement:

•

Amount of tax collected; and/or

•

Such other particulars as may be prescribed.

♦

It may be noted that no provision has been made to provide for any deterrent for not furnishing the Statement or for not furnishing the same within the time prescribed. Further, there is no provision for the recourse, which the payee or buyer may have in such circumstances.

8.4-5 Credit for the tax deducted or collected - The provision in relation to :—

♦

TDS [section 199(3)], reads as follows: "where any deduction is made. . . on or after the 1st day of April, 2005 and paid to the Central Government, the amount of tax deducted and specified in the statement referred to in section 203AA shall be treated as tax paid on behalf of the person referred to in sub-section (1) . . . and credit shall be given to him for the amount so deducted in the assessment... without production of certificate." (Emphasis supplied)

♦

TCS [first proviso to section 206C(4)] reads: "provided that where any amount is collected... on or after 1st day of April, 2005 and paid... to the credit of the Central Government, the amount of tax collected and specified in statement referred to... shall be deemed as payment of tax on behalf of the person from whom the amount has been collected and credit shall be given to him for the amount so collected in the assessment... without production of certificate." (Emphasis supplied)

Thus, the amount of tax deducted/collected and specified in the Statement would be treated as tax paid on behalf of the payee/buyer. It appears, the payee/buyer would get credit for such tax deducted/collected on his/her behalf. For whatever reasons, the amount of tax deducted/collected is not specified in the Statement, the amount not specified would not be treated as tax deducted/collected on behalf of the payee/buyer and credit will not be available for the same to the payee/buyer.

In this connection an issue may arise about the treatment of tax deducted or collected and specified in the statement but not paid by the payer/collector. If appears that to the extent tax deducted/collected, whether specified in the statement or not the recovery cannot be enforced against the payee/buyer, for the following reasons :

(i)

Section 203AA and second proviso to section 206C(5), respectively provide that the prescribed income-tax authorities or authorised person shall prepare and collect the statement of tax deducted/paid [under section 192(1A)] on tax collected.

(ii)

Section 199(3) and first proviso to section 206C(4) treat the tax deducted or collected and specified in the statement as tax paid on behalf of the payee or buyer. Thus, the tax deducted on collected, whether paid or not is the relevant amount which can be considered as paid on behalf of the payee/buyer.

(iii)

Section 205 of the Act provides that where the tax is deductible at source under applicable provisions of Chapter XVII, the assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income;

(iv)

Section 191 contemplates direct payment by the payee only in a case where tax is deducted in terms of Chapter XVII and not in a case where the tax is deducted and not paid.

While claiming the credit, the payee or the buyer may face some difficulties on account of one or more of the following illustrative situations :

♦

The Statement is not received from the prescribed income-tax authority or authorised agency in time. In that case, his return of income would be delayed, with attendant consequences. Alternatively, he may not be able to claim credit for the same.

FACT: ■

The petitioner-assessee had advanced a loan to Ninex at an agreed rate of interest and interest was remitted to assessee, albeit, after deducting tax at source by Ninex. When the assessee filed its return of income, it initially did not claim credit for the tax at source deducted and credit for tax at source was claimed by the assessee in its revised return.

■

The revised return was processed under section 143(1), whereby the credit for tax at source was disallowed.

■

An application under section 154 was filed and the same was rejected.In order to get credit of tax at source deducted by Ninex, the assessee had preferred a representation which was, however, rejected with the observation that as per Form 26AS no credit was reflecting.

■

In instant writ petition, the assessee had sought a direction for being given credit of tax deducted at source by Ninex.

HELD: ■

Ninex is, presently, undergoing a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (“CIRP”). It is also not in dispute that the Resolution Professional (“RP”) has issued a certificate dated 05-01-2021 evidencing that Tax at Source (TAS) amounting to Rs.26,99,950/-, was, in fact, deducted against interest paid by Ninex qua the loan extended to it. [Paras 13 and 14]

■

No recovery towards Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) can be made against the petitioner i.e., the deductee, in view of the provisions of section 205. [Para 21]

■

Insofar as the second issue is concerned, the argument advanced on behalf of the revenue is that no credit for tax can be given having regard to the provisions of section 199. In other words, the submission is that unless the tax deducted at source is “paid” to the Central Government, no credit can be given to the deductee, i.e., the petitioner in this case. As would be evident upon perusing the judgment rendered in Sanjay Sudan v. Asstt. CIT [2023] 148 taxmann.com 329/292 Taxman 138/452 ITR 107 (Delhi) this very submission was rejected. [Para 21.1]

■

Since repeated arguments are raised by the revenue based on the provisions of section 199, the rationale provided in Sanjay Sudan’s case is required to be elaborated. It is required to be emphasized that deduction of taxes at source is one of the methods of collecting tax. The TDS deducted at source is part of the assessee’s income and, therefore, the gross amount is included in the total income and offered to tax. It is on this premise that the tax deducted at source would have to be treated as tax paid on behalf of the assessee. The TDS is deducted prior to the assessment being completed. Thus, it is only when the relevant previous year is over, can the assessee’s total income from all sources be determined. Upon assessment of the total income, amongst others, credit for tax deducted at source is extended to an assessee. If the tax assessed is more than the tax deducted at source, the assessee is granted refund. However, if the tax assessed is less than the tax dedudcted at source, the assessee, i.e., the deductee is liable to pay the deficit amount. [Para 21.2]

■

A perusal of section 4(2) would reveal that in respect of income chargeable to tax, income-tax shall be deducted at source or paid in advance, where it is so required under the provisions of the Act. [Para 17]

As per the provisions of section 201(1), a person responsible to deduct tax, if does not deduct tax or if, after so deducting, fails to deposit the same with the Income-tax Department, then such person is deemed to be an assessee-in-default in respect of such tax. Further as per the provisions of sub-section (1A), such an assessee, who fails to deduct TDS or fails to deposit the same in time, is liable to pay simple interest at the rate as prescribed therein to the Central Government and further as per the sub-section (2) to section 201, such amount of TDS along with simple interest thereon as referred to sub-section (1A) shall be a charge upon the assets of the person responsible. Therefore, by way of such deeming fiction, TDS though deductible from the income of the payee, becomes the tax liability of the deductor and the non-deduction or non-depositing of the same would put such person responsible/deductor in the category of tax defaulter and such tax, though leviable on the income of the payee, along with interest, becomes a charge upon the property of such person responsible/deductor. Further, as per the provisions of section 4, the deduction of tax at source is one of the modes of recovery of charge of income tax. Thus statute has casted a duty upon the payer to deduct tax on behalf of Government of India on the payment made to a payee on which such tax is liable to be deducted as per the provisions of the Act and further such deductor is required to deposit the said tax with the Central Government, failing to do so declares such a person as a defaulter of taxas if of his own tax liability by way of the deeming fiction of section 201. Therefore, under the circumstances, no such defense is available to the person responsible/deductor it to say that it was the liability of the other person. Even though, as per the relevant provisions, if the payee takes into account the said receipts for the purpose of computation of income and pays tax thereupon and files return of income, then such person responsible/deductor is absolved of the liability of payment of tax which he was liable to deduct and deposit but he is not absolved from the payment of interest for the period of default from the date from which such tax was liable to be deducted and the date on such tax was actually paid by the deductee/payee. This liability has been statutorily fastened upon such deductor/payer and it cannot be said to be a business expenditure of the payer.

Further, the carrying on or continuation of business by such deductor/payer is not dependent upon the payment of tax as non-payment of tax does not bar a person from continuation of his business nor the discontinuation of business absolves such a person from payment of tax liability. Such tax liability of the deductor, though, may arise in the course of business but nonetheless, this is not the expenditure for the purpose of business. To explain in a simple way, the payment to the contractor/payee may be a business expenditure but the income tax upon such payment is not the business expenditure, either of the deductor or of the deductee. Therefore, the payment of tax cannot be said to be an expenditure incurred solely and exclusively for the purpose of business or profession of the assessee nor can be the interest thereupon.

In CIT v. South India Corporation Ltd. [2000] 242 ITR 114 (Ker.), the High Court held that the amount is deductible only if the assessee credits the amount to the employee's account in the relevant fund on or before the date, by which he is legally or contractually required to do so. The right to deduction would be lost even if the sum is credited after the due date.

In view of the said decision, the order of the Tribunal was to be set aside and the order of the assessing authority to be restored.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

Section 205, read with  section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Scope of provision) - Assessment years 2009-10, 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Employer paid salary to assessee after deduction of tax at source but did not deposit same with department - Assessing Officer did not allow credit of tax deducted at source and raised demand against assessee towards tax and interest - Whether assessee having accepted salary after deduction of tax at source had no further control over it and it was duty of employer to pay deducted tax to department and employer having failed to perform his duty to deposit deducted tax, assessee could not be penalized - Held, yes - Whether section 199 could not operate as impediment to grant relief to assessee and, thus, impugned demand deserved to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Instruction No. 275, dated 1-6-2015; Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016 and Press Release, dated 11-3-2016

The moment 'S' had reversed the entries with regard to the cost of tickets as well as the commission, it would indicate that no TDS was deducted on behalf of the assessee. If 'S' had wrongly made the payment after deducting the amount, then it was for that company to claim the benefit. How could the assessee claim the credit of TDS? The amount had not gone from the assessee's pocket. Therefore, it could not be repaid to it. This ground taken by the assessee was, therefore, to be rejected. [Para 25]

■

The case turns on a simple but significant proposition. When tax has in fact been deducted at source from the assessee’s receipts, can credit be denied merely because the deductor has not deposited the tax or has not correctly reported it and, therefore, the credit does not surface in Form 26AS. The answer must be in the negative. Section 205 erects a clear bar against making a direct demand on the assessee to the extent tax has been deducted at source from his income. The moment deduction is shown on the strength of primary evidence, the embargo of section 205 attaches and the deductee cannot again be called upon to bear the burden. [Para 19]

■

This statutory position is not only plain on the text of the provision but also reinforced by the Central Board of Direct Taxes. In Instruction No. 275/29/2014-IT(B) dated 1-6-2015 the Board recorded that taxpayers were being denied credit because deductors failed to deposit the tax, and directed that in such cases coercive recovery should not be enforced from the deductee. The subsequent Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016 reiterated the same position and directed field officers not to enforce demands created on account of mismatch of credit due to non-payment by the deductor. These directions are binding on the Department and are intended precisely to avoid double taxation of an innocent deductee. [Para 20]

■

On facts, the assessee has demonstrated deduction of tax at source through its invoices and bank statements. The reconciliation placed on record shows, among others, deduction by Future Retail Limited of a substantial sum which was not deposited owing to the company’s financial condition. In the case of MEP Infraprojects the deposited tax is now reflected on update of 26AS, which only underscores that the mismatch was the consequence of deductor side compliance and not any infirmity in the assessee’s claim. For the remaining parties too the Department has not disputed the services rendered or the gross receipts; its sole objection is non-appearance in 26AS. That objection, in the face of section 205, the CBDT directions and the binding precedents, cannot prevail. [Para 23]

■

It is important to remember that the assessee has already brought the corresponding income to tax. Denial of credit in the assessee’s hands, because the deductor failed to deposit or misreported the deduction, results in taxing the same income twice. Section 205 is the Parliamentary safeguard against precisely such injustice. The Board’s Instruction and Memorandum translate that safeguard into administrative practice. The High Courts have given it judicial benediction. The revenue’s proper remedy lies against the defaulting deductor under sections 200 and 201 and other enabling provisions, and not against the deductee who has already suffered deduction. [Para 24]

■

The revenue suggested that section 199 contemplates credit only on payment to the Government and hence the absence of 26AS entries should defeat the claim. Section 199 cannot be read in isolation. It must be read harmoniously with section 205. Section 199 allocates the time and manner of giving credit in the ordinary course when the deductor has discharged his obligation. Section 205 steps in to prevent a second exaction from the deductee when that ordinary course is derailed by the deductor’s default. The harmonious reading preserves both provisions and avoids the manifest unfairness that would otherwise ensue. [Para 25]

■

The view that the assessee must first secure rectification of the deductors’ e-TDS statements and only thereafter obtain credit cannot be subscribed to. The statute does not impose such a pre-condition. The deductee has neither control over nor access to the deductor’s filings. The insistence effectively makes the assessee hostage to another’s compliance and empties section 205 of content. The more correct and lawful approach is to verify the assessee’s primary evidence of deduction and allow credit accordingly, leaving the Department free to pursue the defaulting deductors in accordance with law. [Para 26]

■

In the result the assessee is entitled to credit of TDS to the extent deduction from its receipts is established on the basis of the contemporaneous material placed on record. The denial of credit by Assessing Officer and its affirmation by the first appellate authority are set aside. The Assessing Officer is directed to verify the assessee’s reconciliation with reference to the invoices, payment advices and bank statements already on record and to allow the corresponding credit of TDS. This direction is squarely in line with section 205, CBDT Instruction dated 1-6-2015 and Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016, and the principles laid down by the Bombay and Delhi High Courts noticed above. [Para 27]

The assessee-company employed a Canadian national 'G' at a fixed remuneration with the perquisites of rent-free accommodation, car with driver and a servant. 'G' filed his tax return and paid taxes after self-assessment. The Assessing Officer noticed from a perusal of the bank account of the employee and the TDS return filed by the assessee that no salary had been paid to the employee nor any deduction under section 192 made by the assessee. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, held that the assessee was in default under sections 201 and 201(1A). Consequently, the Assessing Officer determined the liability arising on account of interest. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had paid the salary to 'G', the expatriate employee through its partner abroad but subsequently when the revenue started surveys, the assessee in an attempt to get out of the mess took the plea that it had not made any such payment and that no tax at source was deductible. The Commissioner, therefore, directed the Assessing Officer to give credit to the taxes paid by 'G' and recover the remaining account including interest from the assessee. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the obligation to deduct tax at source did not arise as the salary payable to 'G' had not been actually paid to him and, therefore, the assessee was not liable to either pay tax under section 201 or interest under section 201(1A).

On appeal :

On facts, it appeared to be a case where, in all probability, the amount was deducted at source by the agency from the prize money payable to the assessee but the same did not seem to have been made over to the Government treasury for payment to the Central Government.

A certificate of deduction is to be provided by the person deducting the tax as provided under section 203. There is a bar against direct demand on the assessee where the tax is deducted at source as provided under section 205. The assessee is not supposed to do any thing in the whole transaction except that he has to accept the payment of the reduced amount from which is deducted income-tax at source. The responsibility to deposit the amount deducted at source as tax is that of the person who is responsible to deduct the tax at source. On the amount being deducted, the assessee only gets a certificate to that effect by the person responsible to deduct the tax. In a case where the amount has been deducted by the person responsible to deduct the amount under the statutory provisions, the assessee has no control over the matter. In case of default in making over the amount to the account of the Central Government, it is obviously the person responsible to deduct or the person who has made the deduction who is held responsible for the same. The responsibility of such person is to the extent that he has to be deemed to be an assessee-in-default in respect of the tax.

The amount of tax can be recovered by the department treating the person responsible to deduct tax at source as an assessee-in-default in respect of the tax. It will not be possible to proceed to recover the amount of tax from the assessee. The assessee cannot be doubly saddled with the tax liability. Deduction of tax at source is only one of the modes of recovery of tax. Once this mode is adopted and by virtue of the statutory provisions the person responsible to deduct the tax at source deducted the amount, only that mode should be pursued for the purpose of recovery of tax liability and the assessee should not be subjected to other modes of recovery of tax by recovering the amount once again to satisfy the tax liability.

In the light of the matter, the notices issued under section 226(3) to the bankers of the assessee to satisfy the tax liability from his bank account were illegal. It was not that the Income-tax Department was helpless in the matter. The person responsible to deduct the tax at source would move into the shoes of the assessee and he would be deemed to be an assessee- in-default. Whatever process or coercive measures were permissible under the law would only be taken against such person and not the assessee.

However, this would not mean that mere deduction of the tax amount at source would amount to total discharge of the tax liability so long as the amount deducted is not deposited in the coffers of the Central Government. According to section 199, credit for tax deducted is to be given when the amount is deducted and paid to the Central Government and a certificate of deduction is produced as furnished under section 203. There was no force in the assessee's submission that on mere deduction of the amount at source, credit for tax must be given and it could not be withheld even though the person responsible to deduct the tax at source had not made it over to the Central Government. Once credit on account of payment of tax is given, the tax liability will stand discharged. Any step to recover the amount of tax can be taken only in case the tax liability is not discharged and it still subsists. The note appended by the Assessing Officer in the order of assessment made it clear that credit for the amount deducted was not being given and that would be given only when evidence as to actual payment of the amount to the Central Government was furnished. But this position would not legally justify initiation of recovery proceedings against the assessee from whose income-tax had been deducted at source. The statutory scheme evolved to employ this mode of recovery of tax at source also points to the same position and rightly so. Section 201 aptly provides that the person responsible to deduct the tax would be deemed to be an assessee-in-default so that he can be proceeded against for recovery of the amount instead of the assessee who has already parted with the amount but due to some commission or omission on the part of the person responsible to deduct the amount at source over whose activity he has no control, he cannot be subjected to double payment of tax and brunt of arduous recovery proceedings. The provisions as contained in section 201 provide a kind of protection to the assessee where tax liability as standing against him is yet discharged and credit for the amount deducted cannot be given in terms of section 199.

For short deduction of tax at source from salaries paid to employees, the ITO levied interest on the assessee from the date of default to the date of payment, but the Commissioner (Appeals) held that interest was chargeable only up to the date of expiry of the limitation period prescribed for com-mencing recovery proceedings in section 231.

HELD: The assessee had filed few payslips that was for the month of April to July 2001 and from its perusal, it appeared that TDS was deducted at the time of payment and the net amount showed in the payslips was credited to the bank account of the assessee. Rule 30 prescribes time limit under various circumstances for payment of tax deducted at source to the credit of Central Government. In case of a person deducting tax at source on behalf of the Government, the tax deducted at source is to be deposited/ credited to the credit of Central Government on the same date. In case of deduction by or on behalf of persons other than Government in respect of sums deducted in accordance with the provision of sections 193, 194A, 194C, 194D, 194E, 194G, 194H, 194-I, 194J, 195, 196, 196B, 196C and 196D and where such sums are credited by a person to the account of payee as on the date up to which accounts of such persons are made, the taxes so deducted shall be deposited/credited within two months after expiration of the month in which that date falls. In any other case, the tax so deducted shall be deposited / credited to the Central Government within one week from the last day of the month in which the deduction is made. In case of any failure either to deduct and pay or having deducted failed to pay such tax provisions of section 201 will be pressed into operation. [Para 7.2]

From plain reading of provisions of section 201 it is clear that section 201 enacts a three-fold punishment for a person, including a company bound to deduct tax at source and pay to the credit of the Central Government and defaulting to do so deduct tax or, after having deducted, defaulting in making payment thereof to the credit of the Central Government. Firstly, the defaulter is treated as an assessee in default and is liable to pay a penalty under section 221. Secondly, he is liable to pay interest on the amount of such tax from the date on which such tax is deductible to the date when such tax is actually paid. The third consequence is that it creates a statutory charge upon all assets of the defaulter for the amount of tax deducted and not paid, plus the amount of interest leviable under section 201(1A). [Para 7.3]

The proviso to section 201(1) states that no penalty shall be charged under section 221 from a defaulting person, unless the Assessing Officer is satisfied that such person, without good and sufficient reasons has failed to deduct and pay such tax. The words 'has without good and sufficient reasons failed to deduct and pay the tax' have been employed by the Legislature in proviso to section 201. Therefore, the benefit of words 'good and sufficient reason' enshrined in proviso will be available to such defaulting persons who failed to deduct and pay such tax and not to the persons who having deducted taxes failed to pay such taxes within the time prescribed by the law. Therefore, in case of persons who have deducted tax as per provisions of law but failed to make payments within the time prescribed they will be visited by all the three consequences. [Para 7.4]

Penalty under section 221(1) is leviable in case of an assessee who is in default or is deemed to be in default in making payment of tax. In case of assessee who is in default three stages i.e. fixation of liability, computation of income and tax payable thereon, and service of demand notice under section 156 on the assessee calling upon him to make payment should have been over. The Calcutta High Court in the case of CIT v. Black Wood Hodge India (P.) Ltd. [1971] 81 ITR 807 has held that it has to be assumed that three stages i.e. fixation of liability, computation of income and tax payable thereon and service of demand notice on the assessee calling upon him to make payment were over. It is only when all these three stages had passed and the assessee fails to comply with the notice of demand that he can become an assessee in default. Therefore, while dealing with the legal fiction introduced by expression 'deemed to be an assessee in default' it would be necessary to assume all those facts on which alone the fiction can operate were over and there had been a failure on the part of the assessee to comply with the notice of demand. [Para 8]

Section 201(1A) provides that a person who either does not deduct or after deduction fails to pay tax as required by or under the Act shall be liable to pay simple interest at the prescribed rate on the amount of tax. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee deducted tax from the salary of the employees and thereafter failed to deposit the tax within the prescribed time. Because of this infraction of law, the assessee was treated as an assessee-in-default and the procedure for recovery contemplated under the Act was invoked Section 201 enacts a three-fold punishment for a person including a company bound to deduct tax at source and defaulting to so deduct tax or, after having deducted, defaulting in making payment thereof to the credit of the Central Government. Firstly, the defaulter is treated as an assessee-in-default and is liable to pay a penalty under section 221. Secondly, he is liable to pay interest on the amount of such tax from the date on which such tax was deductible to the date when such tax is actually paid The third consequence is that it creates a statutory charge upon all the assets of the defaulter for the amount of tax deducted and not paid plus the amount of interest leviable under section 201(1A). Therefore, it was not a part of the salary of the employees which was withheld It was tax on salary of the employees which was deducted but not paid. Had it not been deducted by the employer, the employees would have paid the tax themselves.

Further, under section 203 every person deducting tax in accordance with the provisions of the relevant section of the Act is required to furnish a certificate, inter alia, to the concerned person to the effect that tax has been deducted and specifying the amount so deducted, and the rate at which tax has been deducted at source. Therefore, what had been deducted was tax and it did not retain the character of salary although such deduction had been made from the salary. The character and quality of interest payable for non-compliance with the provisions of the Act would be the same, whether it was levied for non-submission of return in time or non-payment of tax within the prescribed time or for any other reason. Regarding the admissibility of interest as deduction, it has been held in National Engg. Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1978] 113 ITR 252 (Cat) that interest paid under section 220(2) of the Act for delayed payment of taxes is not allowable as deduction in computation of the total income.

Therefore, whenever interest is charged under the Act, whether for delayed payment of tax or for filing under-estimate of tax or for non-submission of the estimate or return or for default in filing return within the time or delay in making payment of tax, it cannot be allowed as deduction in computing total income as essentially such interest is inextricably connected with the amount of income-tax. Where income-tax itself is not a deductible amount, any amount payable in addition to tax, be it compensation or be it penalty, cannot be allowed as a deduction in computing total income.

Hence, interest charged from the assessee under section 201(1A) was not deductible in computing the total income of the assessee.

FACT: The assessee’s employer paid salary to him after deducting the tax therefrom. But despite repeated requests made by the assessee, his employer did not furnish the requisite TDS certificate. Consequently, he filed his return without Form No. 16 and also requested the Assessing Officer to enforce the issue of said certificate by the employer in exercise of his jurisdiction over the matter. However, in the absence of the same, the Assessing Officer framed the assessment under section 143(1)(a) raising tax demand in respect of salary income which was levied for the TDS certificate not furnished as well as interest payable in respect of the said tax. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that in the absence of Form No. 16 and Form No. 24, giving credit for TDS on salary did not appear to be justified, though the assessee could not be asked to pay the tax again to the extent to which tax had already been deducted in view of section 205. He, accordingly, directed the Assessing Officer to ask the assessee to obtain the same from the employer and furnish the same.

On second appeal :

HELD: Tax had been deducted from the salary of the assessee by the employer. In this view of the factual position, section 205 really put a bar against direct demand on the assessee. The interest leviable in respect of TDS also is a consequence of non-furnishing of certificate by the assessee in respect of TDS. Had the employer given the assessee a TDS certificate, no interest could be levied on the assessee as the same was to be reduced while computing assessed tax. However, at the same time, credit for tax deducted at source cannot be given to an assessee unless the assessee submits certificate as prescribed under section 203 in respect of TDS as per provisions of section 199. [Para 5]

Hence, in view of section 205, the authorities under no circumstances could make the assessee liable to make payment of any tax to the extent to which the tax had been deducted at source by the person paying the salary to the assessee under section 192. However, as TDS certificate had not been given by deductor, the credit of TDS could not be given. Under the peculiar circumstances of the case, the income-tax authorities were directed not to recover any tax levied on the assessee in respect of non-furnishing of TDS certificate. There are various provisions in the Act which provide the powers to the income-tax authorities to enforce the payment of tax by deductor and also enforce issue of certificate in respect thereof to the payee. There was no material on record to show that whether such powers had been exercised by the department to enforce the payment of tax deducted at source and also for the issue of certificate thereof. In that view of the situation, the assessee could not be held liable for the consequences which were beyond the control of the assessee, i.e., non-furnishing of TDS certificate. Till such powers were not exercised by the revenue authorities to corner the deductor of tax, i.e., to collect payment of TDS from him and also to obtain the certificate, no tax as well as interest pertaining thereto could be recovered from the assessee. The appeal filed by the assessee was to be allowed in the aforesaid terms. [Para 6]

Thus, provisions of interest u/s 201 are mandatory and automatic and interest has to be paid from date on which tax was deductible till date on which tax is actually paid [CIT v. Even if assessee was bona fide in not making such deduction, it was liable to pay interest [Sun Outsourcing Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2018] 92 taxmann.com 339 (AP)].

Interest u/s 201(1A) is leviable even where recipient is a loss-making company [CIT v. Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board [2011] 14 taxmann.com 73/202 Taxman 454 (Mad.)]. Where tax has already been paid by deductee, no further tax can be collected by deductor, however, interest can be charged from deductor from date of its liability till date of actual tax payment by deductee [S. A. A. Ispahani Trust v. ITO [2013] 34 taxmann.com 29/216 Taxman 1 (Mad.)].

Though Form 26AS (read with rule 31AB and sections 203AA and 206C(5)) represents a part of a wholesome procedure designed by the Revenue for accounting of TDS (and TCS), the burden of proving as to why the said Form (Statement) does not reflect the details of the entire tax deducted at source for and on behalf of a deductee cannot be placed on an assessee-deductee. The assessee, by furnishing the TDS certificate/s bearing the full details of the tax deducted at source, credit for which is being claimed, has discharged the primary onus on it toward claiming credit in its respect. He, accordingly, cannot be burdened any further in the matter. The revenue is fully entitled to conduct proper verification in the matter and satisfy itself with regard to the veracity of the assessee’s claim/s, but cannot deny the assessee credit in respect of TDS without specifying any infirmity in its claim/s.

Form 26AS is a statement generated at the end of the revenue, and the assessee cannot be in any manner held responsible for any discrepancy therein or for the non-matching of TDS reflected therein with the assessee’s claim/s. Where so, no doubt a matter of concern, is one which is to be investigated and pursued by the revenue, which is suitably armed by law therefor. The plea that the deductor may have specified a wrong TAN, so that the TDS may stand reflected in the account of another deductee, is no reason or ground for not allowing credit for the TDS in the hands of the proper deductee. The onus for the purpose lies squarely at the door of the revenue. [Para 4.3]

Therefore, the revenue is obliged to grant the assessee credit for the TDS of which he is able to satisfactorily prove to the Assessing Officer, the factum of deduction of tax at source and its deposit to the credit of the Central Government, subject of course to the conditions of sections 198 and 199. The Assessing Officer is accordingly directed to allow the assessee credit for the impugned shortfall, subject to the said verification/s and condition/s.

It was observed that the assessee himself namely Anirudh Bhuwalka has been MD and CEO of the AMW Motors. The assessee was the overall in charge and final authority of the said company. In other words, to say that the affairs of the AMW Motors were managed by the assessee, himself. The assessee himself was responsible for payment of salary to the staff as well as to himself and also for deduction of TDS, if any. On the one hand, the assessee himself acting as the MD and CEO of AMW Motors, did not deduct the TDS on the salary paid/payable to himself for working as MD and CEO of the company and on the other hand, the assessee is pleading that he is entitled to the adjustment of the TDS which in fact was never deposited by his company. The assessee is claiming exemption from taxation on his salary income stating that his employer i.e. AMW company was supposed to deposit the TDS, whereas the assessee, himself, being the principal officer and administrative head of the company was supposed to ensure the deposit of TDS, not only on this own salary but also in respect of salary of other employees. [Para 11]

The assessee in this case has put a claim against the department of set-off of the TDS against tax demand which was never deposited by the assessee acting as employer of himself and thus cannot be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong or default. It is pertinent to note here that the assessee being the managing director of the company himself was liable to file and verify the income tax return on behalf of the company as per the provisions of section 140(c). Further, even if an action is brought against the company for non-deduction of TDS even then the assessee being the principal officer of the company is liable to be treated as assessee-in-default under the provisions of section 201(1) and 201(1a) read with section 204 and even as per the provisions of section 271C, it would be the assessee being the managing director and the principal officer of the company who would be liable to be prosecuted under section 271C for default in deduction of TDS or non-deposit of TDS. Therefore, even otherwise, if the taxes to be recovered from the company, it will be the assessee who will be liable on behalf of the company to pay the taxes and interest thereupon including liable to be tried under Penal provisions for non-deduction/non-deposit of tax on his own salary. In other words, the assessee being the managing director and chief executive officer of the company himself is the principal officer/person responsible for all acts of defaults in non-deduction/non-deposit of TDS and under such circumstances, he cannot be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong. [Para 12]

The assessee is not entitled to any claim of set-off of TDS, which was never deposited by the company, the assessee being the principal officer and overall administrative head of the company, out of his own act and conduct. There is no merit in the appeal of the assessee and the same is accordingly dismissed. [Para 13]

time for taking an action under a particular section largely depends on a host of factors, inter alia, the nature of proceedings; the character of the order, etc. In order to determine the reasonable time for taking an action under section 201, it is important to have a look at such necessary factors. [Para 14.4]

VI. Nature of proceedings under section 201(1)

The following steps are involved in the proceedings for deduction, payment and recovery of tax at source : When a person pays a sum to anyone on which tax is required to be deducted, then the person responsible for paying such sum is under an obligation to deduct tax at source at the time of credit of such sum to the account of the payee or at the time of payment thereof in cash or by issuing of a cheque or by any other mode, whichever is earlier. When the person responsible has deducted the tax and paid it to the credit of the Central Government or as the Board directs him, his duty is over insofar as the question of deduction of tax at source is concerned, of course, subject to the issuance of certificate of such deduction to the payee and the furnishing of the TDS return in time. If, however, such person who is responsible for deducting tax at source fails to deduct the whole or any part of the tax deductible or after deducting fails to pay the same to the exchequer, prima facie, he becomes the assessee-in-default. The very act of not deducting tax at source or failure to deposit the same makes such person as an assessee-in-default. [Paras 15.1 and 15.2]

When there is such a failure as is referred to in the preceding para, the proceedings are launched against the person responsible and inquiry is conducted. If at the conclusion of such proceedings, it is found that the person responsible for paying has failed to deduct tax or has failed to deposit the same after deduction, he or it is deemed to be an assessee-in-default in respect of such tax by way of an order under section 201(1) subject to the prescription of the Explanation to section 191. Thus, this order crystallizes the liability on the person responsible for paying tax which was deductible. Albeit the person responsible for deducting tax at source becomes a defaulter the moment he makes the payment or credits it to the account of the payee, whichever is earlier, without deduction of tax at source, but on the passing of the order under section 201(1), the amount of tax is determined in respect of which such person responsible is deemed to be an assessee-in-default. [Para 15.3]

On the passing of the order under section 201(1), a notice of demand is issued under section 156 in the name of such person who is deemed to be an assessee-in-default, specifying the sum so payable. If the notice of demand is complied with and the sum determined by way of an order under section 201(1), is paid, the matter ends. [Para 15.4]

If, however, there is a failure to comply with the terms of notice of demand issued under section 156, the tax recovery proceedings are initiated. Section 231, prior to its omission by the Direct Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 1987 with effect from 1-4-1989, provided that no proceedings for the recovery of any sum payable under this Act would be commenced after the expiration of three years from the last day of the financial year in which the demand was made or in the case of a person who was deemed to be an assessee-in-default under any provisions of this Act. This section, thus, provides that no proceedings for recovery of any sum payable under this Act shall be commenced after the expiry of three years from the last day of the financial year in which the demand was made. This means that the recovery certificate could be issued by the Assessing Officer only within the aforesaid period of three years. Simultaneous with the omission of section 231, an amendment has been carried out to section 222 by which the requirement of the issue of such certificate by an Assessing Officer has been dispensed with and the TRO can now draw the statement of arrears and assume jurisdiction as soon as the assessee is in default. [Para 15.5]

On scrutiny of Form No. 24 filed by the assessee-company for the assessment year 1989-90, the Assessing Officer observed that net taxable salary of K, an employee of the assessee, was Rs. 54,240 whereon tax of Rs. 11,493 was to be deducted at source but the assessee had deducted only an amount of Rs. 9,000. The Assessing Officer, therefore, directed the assessee to pay an amount of Rs. 2,493 plus interest thereon and he also initiated penalty proceedings. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the view of the Assessing Officer. The assessee’s case was that K had intimated the office that he would be depositing Rs. 20,000 in NSS as before but the assessee did not deposit the said amount and this misleading intimation resulted in short deduction of tax and there being no intentional default on the part of the assessee interest could not be levied on it and, further, since the employee had already paid short deducted tax, the assessee was not liable to make payment of short deducted tax.

It has been held by the Supreme Court in the case of All India Reporter Ltd. v. Ramchandra D. Datar [1961] 41 ITR 446 that where an employee obtains a decree for arrears of salary, compensation for wrongful termination of service and salary due for the period of notice and also interest and costs, there is no scope for applying the provision for deduction of income-tax at source. The amount is payable as 'judgment-debt' and not as 'salary' and the judgment-debtor cannot claim to deduct income-tax payable as salary.

Accordingly, the contention of the respondent had to be upheld. However, the appellant would be at liberty to take steps for recovery of the amount of tax paid to the credit of the respondent in accordance with law.

It is now clear from the provisions of the Act that the assessee from whom income-tax has been deducted at source in accordance with the provisions contained in the Act, is entitled to credit of the said tax irrespective of whether the person deducting the tax has credited the same to the Central Government or not. The person deducting the tax at source is in a sense statutory agent of the Central Government and for his default assessee cannot be made to suffer. The words used in section 199 ‘and paid to the Central Government’, in the context mean ‘payable to the Central Government’. In this view of the matter the assessee in the instant case was entitled to the deduction of tax deducted at source.

FACT: ■

The assessee, law firm, was engaged in providing legal services. The assessee received payments from clients which were net of tax deducted at source, the deductors having withheld the applicable TDS before releasing amounts. The assessee while filing return claimed credit for such deductions while offering the entire gross receipts to tax.

■

The Assessing Officer denied credit of TDS solely on the ground that such amounts did not feature in Form No. 26AS. Consequently, a demand was raised comprising the disallowed TDS together with interest under section 234B and under section 234C.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the denial of credit, holding that unless the deduction appeared in Form 26AS, the assessee could not be allowed relief. As regards levy of interest under sections 234B and 234C, the Commissioner (Appeals) held the same to be consequential and mandatory.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The case turns on a simple but significant proposition. When tax has in fact been deducted at source from the assessee’s receipts, can credit be denied merely because the deductor has not deposited the tax or has not correctly reported it and, therefore, the credit does not surface in Form 26AS. The answer must be in the negative. Section 205 erects a clear bar against making a direct demand on the assessee to the extent tax has been deducted at source from his income. The moment deduction is shown on the strength of primary evidence, the embargo of section 205 attaches and the deductee cannot again be called upon to bear the burden. [Para 19]

the provisions contained in sections 15,16 and 17. The deduction of tax may have to be made at the time of payment of salary but the calculation of the tax deductible will have to be made on the estimated salary income of the employee for the relevant financial ear according to the provision of the Act and the rules framed for this purpose. There is no warrant for the proposition that the amount of income-tax deductible will be calculated only on the amount that is actually handed over to the assessee. That apart, when an employer undertakes to pay tax-free income to an employee, what he undertakes is to pay an agreed sum of money plus the tax payable on that amount. The employee enjoys the benefit of the amount of tax which is paid on his account to the treasury. By this process, the employer discharges the statutory financial obligation of the employee. Therefore, the total salary of the employee must be the amount that is actually paid to him as also the amount of tax which was otherwise payable by him but which has been paid on his account by the company. Otherwise there will not be any difference between an amount of salary which is liable to be diminished by taxation and the same amount of salary which is paid free of tax. The burden of income-tax liability cannot be shifted by agreement. In the instant case, by undertaking to pay tax-free salary, the employer had really agreed to discharge the tax burden of the employee. The amount of tax that was paid by the employer was for and on behalf of the employee. Therefore, the amount of tax payable on the salary income of the employees, which was borne by the assessee, should be treated as part of the salary of the employee for the purpose of making estimate of income of the employee under section 192 and for the employer's failure to do so interest was rightly charged under section 201(1A ).

So far as the argument regarding the responsibility of the person handing overpayment was concerned, the person responsible for paying the salary of an employee is the employer himself. In the instant case, the company was the employer. It had to pay the salaries of its employees. An Officer or a clerk of the company might be engaged to actually hand over the pay cheque or the pay packet to the employees. But such payments were made for and on behalf of the company. The person responsible for payment of the salary was the employer itself. Thus, this argument of the assessee was to be rejected.

As regards the question of limitation, one of the consequences of failure to deduct or pay tax in accordance with the provisions of the Act is that the principal officer and the company shall be deemed to be an assessee in default in respect of the tax under the provisions of section 201. If an assessee is in default or deemed to be in default, the recovery of tax due might be made under the procedure specifically laid down for that purpose under the Act. The recovery could also be made by any other procedure. The period of limitation laid down by section 231 is confined to recovery proceedings under the Act. This provision of limitation could not curtail the power of the Government to file a suit to recover the outstanding amount of tax payable by any other process of law. The outstanding demand of tax could be recovered like any other debt due to the State. Even after the period of limitation laid down in section 231 is over, it is open to the Government to file a suit to recover the outstanding amount of tax subject to the provisions of Limitation Act. Therefore, in the instant case, it could not be said that the amount of tax deducted at source had become irrecoverable being barred by limitation.
